leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months; it is noticeably better on day two, so reheat gently over low heat and thin with a splash of broth.

title: Yucatecan Sopa de Lima with Crisp Tortilla Strips
blurb: A clear, allspice-scented chicken broth blasted with charred lime and habanero, poured over a nest of tortilla strips fried crisp enough to crackle.

ingredients.item: 6 Casa Mamita corn tortillas, cut in thin strips

steps.text: Season the thighs on both sides with salt and pepper. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a saucepan over medium-high and sear the chicken until the undersides are golden brown, then flip once and pull the pan back to medium.
steps.tip: The browned bits on the bottom give this clear broth its backbone.

steps.text: Push the chicken aside, add the onion and tomatoes with a pinch of salt, and cook until the onion turns translucent and the tomatoes slump into the pan juices.
Stir in the oregano, allspice, and cumin and let them toast until you can smell the allspice clearly. Pour in the broth, add the halved habanero, and bring it to a gentle simmer.
steps.tip: Allspice is the signature note of Yucatecan cooking; do not skip it.

steps.text: Simmer uncovered, skimming any foam, until the chicken is cooked through and shreds easily against the side of the pot with a fork.
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy bubble so the broth stays clear rather than cloudy.

steps.text: While the soup simmers, heat the remaining oil in a skillet over medium-high and fry the tortilla strips in two batches, turning them, until they are stiff and pale gold. Drain them on paper towels and salt them right away.
steps.tip: Pull them a shade before they look done; they darken as they cool.

steps.text: Halve two of the limes and press them cut side down in a dry hot skillet until the surfaces are blackened and the juice inside is hot. Cut the remaining limes into wedges.
steps.tip: Charring pushes the lime from sour to smoky and slightly sweet.

steps.text: Pull the chicken out, shred it in big pieces, and return it to the pot. Fish out the habanero, then kill the heat and squeeze in the juice of the charred limes, tasting as you go until the broth is bracingly sour.
steps.tip: Add the lime off heat so it stays bright instead of turning bitter.

steps.text: Pile a handful of tortilla strips in the bottom of each bowl and ladle the hot soup over them. Finish with cilantro, extra strips on top, and lime wedges for squeezing at the table.
steps.tip: Serve immediately, while the strips still crunch.

swap: No corn tortillas? Fry strips of Casa Mamita flour tortillas or crush in a handful of plain tortilla chips just before serving.
leftovers: Refrigerate the broth and chicken up to 3 days, always storing the fried strips separately at room temperature; reheat the soup and add fresh lime juice each time.

title: Okinawan Pork and Tofu Champuru
blurb: A blistering-hot stir-fry of crisped pork belly, golden torn tofu, and charred cabbage bound with soft egg and finished with a snowdrift of dancing bonito flakes.

ingredients.item: 12 oz pork belly or thick-cut Appleton Farms bacon, cut in 1-inch strips
1/2 head green cabbage, cut in rough 2-inch squares
1 tsp Trader Joe's Mushroom & Company Multipurpose Umami Seasoning Blend
2 packages Trader Joe's Frozen Jasmine Rice

steps.text: Wrap the tofu block in a clean towel, set a heavy pan on top, and let it press while you prep everything else. Tear it into rough bite-size chunks rather than cubing it so the craggy edges catch color.
steps.tip: Torn tofu has more surface area and browns far better than neat cubes.

steps.text: Lay the pork strips in a cold wok or large skillet and set it over medium heat so the fat renders slowly. Cook, stirring occasionally, until the strips are deep brown and crisp at the edges and the pan holds a good slick of fat.
steps.tip: Starting cold renders more fat, which is the cooking medium for everything else.

steps.text: Scoop the pork onto a plate and leave the fat behind. Raise the heat to medium-high and add the tofu chunks in one layer, letting them sit undisturbed until a golden crust forms before turning them.
steps.tip: If you stir too soon the tofu shreds; wait for the release.

steps.text: Push the tofu to one side, beat the eggs with a pinch of salt, and pour them into the empty half. Stir them in loose folds until barely set and still glossy, then slide them out onto the pork plate.
steps.tip: Undercook the eggs here since they finish in the hot pan later.

steps.text: Crank the heat to high and add the cabbage all at once. Let it sit against the metal without stirring so the cut edges blacken and blister, then toss and let it sit again until the leaves are wilted at the ribs but still snapping.
steps.tip: Real wok-style char is the difference between champuru and steamed cabbage.

steps.text: Return the pork and tofu to the pan, then pour in the soy sauce, mirin, sesame oil, and umami seasoning around the edges so they hiss and caramelize. Toss everything hard until the sauce clings and the pan is nearly dry.
steps.tip: Saucing down the hot sides toasts the soy instead of steaming the food.

steps.text: Kill the heat and fold the eggs and scallions back in with a few gentle turns so the egg stays in soft ribbons. Grind over plenty of black pepper.
Heat the jasmine rice according to the package while the pan rests. Serve the champuru over the rice and blizzard the whole thing with bonito flakes, which will curl and wave in the rising steam.
steps.tip: Add the bonito at the very last second so it moves at the table.

swap: No bonito flakes? Stir 1 tsp of instant dashi powder into the sauce and finish with toasted sesame seeds for texture.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat in a screaming-hot dry skillet rather than the microwave so the tofu and pork recrisp, and add fresh bonito on top.

title: Alsatian Coq au Riesling with Bacon and Mushrooms
blurb: Chicken simmered down in dry Riesling until the wine turns into a silky mustard-cream sauce studded with smoky lardons and deeply browned mushrooms.

ingredients.item: 4 slices Appleton Farms bacon, cut in lardons
6 oz wide egg noodles or spaetzle

steps.text: Set a heavy skillet over medium heat and render the lardons, stirring now and then, until they are crisp and have given up a pool of fat. Lift them out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat in the pan.
steps.tip: Start them in a cold pan so they render rather than seize.

steps.text: Pat the thighs dry, season with salt and pepper, and sear them in the bacon fat over medium-high without moving them until the undersides are mahogany. Flip, brown briefly, and move them to a plate; they will finish in the sauce.
steps.tip: You want color, not doneness, at this stage.

steps.text: Add the mushrooms in one layer and leave them completely alone until they stop squeaking, release their water, and take on dark caramelized faces. Salt them only after they have browned.
steps.tip: Salting early pulls out water and stalls the browning.

steps.text: Drop the heat to medium, add the butter, shallots, and thyme, and cook until the shallots go soft and translucent. Sprinkle the flour over everything and stir until it disappears and smells faintly toasty.

Pour in the Riesling and scrape every browned scrap off the bottom of the pan. Let it bubble briskly until it has reduced by about half and the sharp alcohol smell has cooked off, and start your noodle water while you wait.
steps.tip: Taste the wine first; if you would not drink it, do not cook with it.

steps.text: Whisk in the cream and Dijon, then nestle the chicken back in along with its juices. Turn the heat to low and simmer gently, spooning sauce over the thighs, until the sauce coats a spoon and the chicken is cooked through.
steps.tip: Keep it under a boil so the cream stays smooth.

steps.text: Boil the noodles in well-salted water until just tender, drain them, and toss with a knob of butter and a pinch of pepper. Taste the sauce and adjust with salt and a little more mustard if it needs sharpening.

Spoon the noodles into warm shallow bowls, lay the chicken over them, and pour the sauce and mushrooms across the top. Scatter the crisp lardons and parsley over everything just before it goes to the table.
steps.tip: Adding the bacon at the end keeps it crunchy against the sauce.

swap: No Riesling? Any dry, aromatic white such as Pinot Gris or Sauvignon Blanc works; avoid anything oaky or sweet.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat the chicken and sauce covered over low heat with a splash of cream, and cook fresh noodles rather than reheating them.

title: Colombian Chicken Sancocho with Aji Picante
blurb: A golden, cumin-scented pot of fall-apart chicken, corn rounds, green plantain, and potatoes that thicken the broth themselves, served with a fierce green aji on the side.

ingredients.item: 4 lb bone-in skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks (Kirkwood)
2 green plantains, peeled and cut in thick chunks
3 ears corn, cut in 2-inch rounds (or 6 Season's Choice frozen cobbettes)
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut in large chunks
1 large bunch cilantro, stems and leaves separated

steps.text: Season the chicken hard with salt and pepper and pile it into a large stockpot with the onion, half the scallions, the garlic, one whole jalapeno, the cumin, the turmeric, and the cilantro stems. Cover with about 12 cups of cold water.
steps.tip: Starting in cold water draws more flavor out of the bones.

steps.text: Bring the pot to a boil over high heat, then immediately drop it to a bare simmer. Skim off the grey foam that rises in the first few minutes until the surface runs clear.
steps.tip: Skimming now is what gives sancocho its clean golden broth.

steps.text: Cover partially and simmer gently so the surface only trembles, until the chicken is tender enough that the meat pulls back from the bone ends. Taste the broth and season it well with salt.
steps.tip: A hard boil will cloud the broth and dry out the meat.

steps.text: While it simmers, make the aji: finely chop the cilantro leaves, the remaining scallions, and the second jalapeno, then stir them together with the juice of one lime, a splash of water, and a big pinch of salt. Let it sit so the flavors marry.
steps.tip: The aji should taste sharper and saltier than seems reasonable on its own.

steps.text: Add the plantain chunks to the pot and simmer uncovered until they are starting to soften but still hold together firmly at the center when pierced.
steps.tip: Green plantain releases starch that begins thickening the broth.

steps.text: Add the potatoes and corn rounds, pushing them under the liquid, and simmer until the potatoes are completely tender and a few edges have crumbled into the broth, thickening it to a light body.
steps.tip: Those disintegrating potato edges are the goal, not a mistake.

steps.text: Fish out the whole jalapeno and any loose bones, then pull the chicken pieces to a board if you want and slip the skin off. Return the meat to the pot in large pieces and taste the broth one last time for salt.
steps.tip: Leaving big bone-in pieces is traditional; boneless is easier for lunches.

steps.text: Let the pot rest off the heat so the flavors settle and the fat rises to skim if you like. Ladle into wide bowls with a piece of everything in each, and pass the aji and remaining lime wedges at the table.
steps.tip: Every bowl should get chicken, plantain, corn, and potato.

swap: No green plantains? Use 1 lb of frozen yuca chunks or an extra pound of potatoes, added at the same stage.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and the broth thickens considerably as the starch sets; loosen with water or broth when reheating and make a fresh batch of aji, which is best the day it is chopped.

title: Cantonese Steamed Cod with Sizzling Ginger-Scallion Oil
blurb: Silky steamed white fish under a raft of raw ginger and scallion that gets hit with smoking-hot oil at the table, then flooded with sweet soy.

ingredients.item: 2 thick cod or haddock fillets (about 6 oz each)
1 large knob fresh ginger (about 3 inches), half smashed and half julienned
6 scallions, whites smashed and greens finely julienned
3 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
1 tbsp Shaoxing wine or dry sherry
3 tbsp peanut or other neutral high-heat oil
4 heads baby bok choy, halved lengthwise

steps.text: Set a rack or a pair of chopsticks inside a wide lidded skillet or wok, add water to just below the rack, and bring it to a hard boil over high heat. Meanwhile pat the fish completely dry and salt it lightly on both sides.
steps.tip: The plate must sit above the water, never in it

steps.text: Scatter the smashed ginger and scallion whites over a heatproof plate that fits inside the pan, lay the fillets on top, and splash them with the Shaoxing wine. Lower the plate onto the rack, cover, and steam over medium-high.
While the fish steams, drop the julienned ginger and scallion greens into a bowl of cold water so they curl and crisp, then drain them right before serving.
Stir the soy sauce, sugar, and a splash of water together in a small saucepan and warm it over low heat just until the sugar dissolves and the sauce smells round instead of sharp. Keep it hot.

Tuck the bok choy halves around the plate for the last stretch of steaming and microwave the jasmine rice according to the bag. The fish is done when it flakes into thick opaque petals at the very center.
steps.tip: Pull it the moment it flakes, or it turns cottony

steps.text: Lift the plate out carefully and tip off the cloudy pooled liquid, then discard the smashed aromatics underneath. Pile the drained ginger and scallion threads over the fillets.
Heat the peanut oil in a small pan over high heat until it shimmers and a single scallion shred sizzles violently on contact, then pour it straight over the aromatics so the whole plate crackles.
steps.tip: This step is the entire dish, so get the oil truly ripping

steps.text: Pour the warm soy mixture around the base of the fillets rather than over the top, finish with the sesame oil and cilantro, and serve with the rice and bok choy.

swap: No cod at the counter? Any thick, mild white fillet works, and thick-cut salmon steams beautifully with the same treatment.
leftovers: Flake any leftover fish into the sauce and fold it through cold rice the next day for a quick fried rice with extra scallion.

title: Dhaba-Style Chicken Karahi with Crushed Coriander
blurb: A roadside-style karahi where tomatoes are fried down hard until the ghee separates and the chicken wears the masala like a glaze, finished with a fistful of raw ginger.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut into big chunks
1 large knob fresh ginger, half grated and half julienned
2 to 3 green serrano chiles, slit lengthwise
1 tsp Kashmiri chili powder or sweet paprika
1 bunch cilantro, leaves and tender stems chopped

steps.text: Melt the ghee in a wok or heavy skillet over high heat until it ripples and thins out. Add the chicken in a single uncrowded layer and leave it alone until the undersides are browned and the edges have caught color.
steps.tip: Crowding steams the meat and you lose the fond

steps.text: Stir in the crushed coriander seeds, garlic, grated ginger, and slit chiles and toss constantly until the garlic smells sweet and the coriander turns fragrant and toasty.

Add the tomatoes, turmeric, chili powder, and a generous pinch of salt. Cook over medium-high, mashing the tomatoes against the pan every couple of minutes, until they collapse into a thick masala and rust-colored ghee pools at the edges.
steps.tip: Oil separating at the rim means the masala is cooked

steps.text: Splash in a few tablespoons of water, scrape the bottom clean, then cover and drop the heat to medium-low so the chicken finishes through to the center in the steam.
While it cooks, warm the naan directly over a gas flame or in a dry skillet over medium-high, turning it until it puffs and picks up dark blistered spots.
Uncover, raise the heat to high, and stir almost constantly as the sauce tightens, darkens a shade, and clings to each piece of chicken instead of running off it.
steps.tip: This is the bhuna, and it is where the flavor concentrates

steps.text: Kill the heat, shower on the garam masala, the julienned ginger, and most of the cilantro, and let it sit a minute before serving straight from the pan with the naan and the last of the cilantro.

swap: Out of serranos? A couple of jalapenos plus an extra pinch of chili powder gets you close, and boneless breasts work if you cut the covered cooking short.
leftovers: Chop the leftovers fine and pile them into warm naan with raw onion for a next-day roll that beats the original.

title: Sardinian Saffron Sausage Malloreddus with Pecorino
blurb: Ridged little pasta shells in a brick-red sausage ragu perfumed with saffron and wild fennel, buried under a snowdrift of sharp pecorino.

ingredients.item: 12 oz Never Any! Italian sausage, casings removed
8 oz Priano malloreddus, gnocchetti sardi, or small shells

steps.text: Crumble the saffron threads into a small bowl with a few tablespoons of very hot water and leave them to steep while you build the sauce. Put a large pot of heavily salted water on to boil.
steps.tip: The soaking water should turn deep orange

steps.text: Heat a wide skillet over medium-high with a slick of olive oil, add the sausage in one flat slab, and let it sit untouched until the underside is deeply browned before breaking it into craggy pieces.
Add the onion, fennel seeds, and pepper flakes and cook over medium until the onion is soft and translucent, then stir in the garlic for the last minute.
Pour in the white wine, scrape every browned bit off the bottom, and simmer hard until the pan smells sweet rather than boozy and the liquid has nearly disappeared.

Crush the tomatoes to shreds with your hands straight into the pan, add the saffron and its water and a good pinch of salt, and simmer over low, stirring now and then, until the sauce turns dark brick red and mounds on the spoon.
While the sauce reduces, boil the pasta until it is still noticeably firm at the core, then scoop out a mug of the starchy water before draining.
steps.tip: Pull it a minute early since it finishes in the sauce

steps.text: Tip the pasta into the skillet with a splash of pasta water and half the pecorino, and toss over medium heat until the sauce turns glossy and coats every ridge.
Take the pan off the heat, tear in the basil, and serve with the remaining pecorino piled on top.

swap: If saffron is out of reach, a small pinch of turmeric plus the fennel seeds keeps the color and the sweet-savory edge.
leftovers: Sauce and pasta keep together for three days; reheat in a skillet with a splash of water and fresh pecorino to bring the gloss back.

title: Egyptian Chicken Fattah with Garlic-Vinegar Tomato Sauce
blurb: Layers of shattered crisp bread, buttery broth-cooked rice, and burnished chicken, all doused in a sharp garlic-vinegar tomato sauce that cuts straight through the richness.

ingredients.item: 3 lb Kirkwood bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks
10 cloves garlic, half smashed and half finely minced
1 cinnamon stick, 4 green cardamom pods, and 2 bay leaves
2 cups Earthly Grains basmati or long-grain rice
1/4 cup white or red wine vinegar
2 pieces Naan, torn into rough shards

steps.text: Pile the chicken into a large pot with the quartered onion, smashed garlic, cinnamon stick, cardamom, and bay leaves, cover with cold water by an inch, and bring to a boil over high heat. Skim off the gray foam that rises as it comes up.
steps.tip: Skimming is the difference between cloudy and clean broth

steps.text: Drop the heat to a bare simmer, partially cover, and cook until the meat is tender and pulling back from the ends of the bones. Meanwhile rinse the rice under cold water until it runs clear and tear the naan into shards.

Lift the chicken onto a foil-lined sheet pan and strain the broth into a bowl, discarding the spices and keeping the broth hot. Brush the chicken with ghee, salt it, and broil on high until the skin is blistered, brown, and crackling.
In a saucepan, toast the drained rice in a couple tablespoons of ghee over medium heat, stirring, until the grains turn chalky white and smell nutty like popcorn.

Pour in hot strained broth to cover the rice by about a finger's width, season with salt, bring to a boil, then clamp on the lid and cook on the lowest heat until every drop is absorbed. Rest it off the heat, still covered, before fluffing.
steps.tip: No peeking, and no stirring once the lid is on

steps.text: Toss the naan shards with a little ghee on a sheet pan and bake or broil them until they are dry, golden, and audibly crisp when you tap one.

Sizzle the minced garlic with the coriander and cumin in the remaining ghee over medium heat until the garlic is pale gold and sharply fragrant but not browned, then add the tomato sauce and a ladle of broth and simmer until it darkens and thickens.
steps.tip: Browned garlic turns bitter, so pull it early

steps.text: Off the heat, stir the vinegar into the tomato sauce and taste; it should be aggressively tangy. Layer the crisp bread in a wide dish, moisten it with hot broth, pile on the rice and then the chicken, and pour the sauce over everything before showering with parsley.

swap: No naan on hand? Torn pita, split hoagie rolls, or even plain flour tortillas crisp up just as well in the oven.
leftovers: Store the rice, chicken, and sauce separately for up to four days and crisp fresh bread each time you reheat, since soaked bread goes soft overnight.

title: Bavarian Jagerschnitzel with Bacon-Mushroom Gravy
blurb: A pounded-thin pork cutlet fried in foaming butter until the crust puffs away from the meat, served with a dark bacon and mushroom gravy poured alongside so it stays shatteringly crisp.

ingredients.item: 2 boneless pork loin chops (about 1 lb total)
1 tsp Mushroom & Company Multipurpose Umami Seasoning Blend

steps.text: Lay each chop between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound it with a heavy pan from the center outward until it is thin and even all over. Season both sides with salt and pepper.
steps.tip: Thin and even means it cooks through before the crust burns

steps.text: Set out three shallow dishes of flour, beaten egg, and breadcrumbs. Coat each cutlet in flour, then egg, then crumbs, pressing lightly rather than packing them on, and rest them on a rack.
steps.tip: A loose crumb coat is what lets the crust puff

steps.text: Render the bacon in a skillet over medium heat until the fat has pooled and the pieces are crisp and deep brown, then scoop the bacon out and leave the fat behind.

Turn the heat to medium-high, spread the mushrooms in the bacon fat in a single layer, and leave them completely still until the undersides are dark brown. Add the onion and cook until it softens and turns translucent.
steps.tip: Salt the mushrooms only after they brown

steps.text: Sprinkle in the umami seasoning and a spoonful of the leftover flour, stir for a minute, then pour in the broth and scrape the pan clean. Simmer until it reduces by about half, add the cream, and hold it over the lowest heat.

In a second wide skillet, heat a generous layer of olive oil with the butter over medium-high until the butter foams and the foam just begins to subside. Slide in the cutlets and tilt the pan to spoon hot fat over the tops as they fry.
Flip once the underside is even golden brown and cook the second side until it matches and the crust has visibly lifted away from the meat in blisters.
Rest the cutlets on a rack for a minute so they stay crisp, stir the bacon back into the gravy, and serve the gravy in a puddle beside each schnitzel with lemon wedges for squeezing.
steps.tip: Gravy on top turns the crust to mush

swap: Thin-pounded chicken breasts or turkey cutlets stand in perfectly, and a splash of extra broth covers for the cream.
leftovers: Reheat leftover cutlets on a rack in a hot oven, never the microwave, and warm the gravy separately with a splash of broth.

title: Uyghur Cumin Lamb with Blistered Onions
blurb: Seared lamb tossed in a blizzard of hand-crushed toasted cumin and chili with charred onions and peppers, scooped up with torn warm naan.

ingredients.item: 1 lb boneless lamb shoulder or leg, sliced thin against the grain
1 large onion, cut into thick wedges and separated
1 green bell pepper, cut into wide strips
2 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
1 tbsp Shaoxing wine or dry sherry

steps.text: Toss the sliced lamb with the soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, and cornstarch until every piece is slick, then leave it to sit while you cut the vegetables.
steps.tip: The cornstarch is what gives you that velvety restaurant texture

steps.text: Toast the cumin seeds in a dry skillet over medium heat, shaking constantly, until they darken a shade and smell sharply fragrant. Tip them onto a board and crush them coarsely with the flat of a knife along with the chili flakes.
steps.tip: Crush, do not grind, so you get crunchy pops of spice

steps.text: Warm the naan in a low oven or dry skillet while the pan comes up to temperature, then wrap it in a towel to stay soft.
Heat a wok or heavy skillet over the highest heat until it faintly smokes, add the oil, and lay the lamb out in one layer. Leave it completely undisturbed so it sears rather than steams.
Stir-fry hard until no pink remains and the edges are crisped and lacquered, then scrape the lamb out onto a plate.
Throw the onion and bell pepper into the same searing pan and let them sit still until the edges blacken and blister before tossing them once or twice; they should stay crunchy in the middle.
Return the lamb with the garlic and most of the crushed cumin and chili, and toss constantly until the spices coat everything and the pan smells overwhelmingly of cumin.
Kill the heat, fold in the cilantro and the last of the spice mix, and serve straight from the pan with the warm naan for tearing and scooping.

swap: Lamb not in the case? Thin-sliced sirloin or skirt steak takes the same treatment, and ground lamb works if you press and brown it in a slab.
leftovers: Pile leftovers into warm naan with raw onion and extra cilantro, or reheat in a screaming hot pan for a minute so the edges re-crisp.

title: Cuban Bistec Encebollado with Black Beans and Rice
blurb: Thin steaks marinated in garlicky citrus mojo and seared hard, then buried under a tangle of onions cooked down in the same pan until syrupy and golden.

ingredients.item: 1 lb thin-cut sirloin or top round steaks
6 cloves garlic, mashed to a paste
small handful cilantro or parsley, chopped

steps.text: Mash the garlic with a big pinch of salt into a paste, then whisk it with the juice of two limes, the juice of the orange, the cumin, and the oregano. That sour-orange mix is your mojo.
Pour half the mojo over the steaks and turn them to coat, then toss the onion rings with the other half in a separate bowl. Let both sit while you cook the beans.
steps.tip: Any longer in the acid and the meat goes chalky

steps.text: Soften the bell pepper in olive oil in a small saucepan over medium heat until it slumps and smells sweet, then add the black beans with their liquid and the bay leaf and simmer until the liquid thickens around them.
Set a cast iron skillet over high heat until it just begins to smoke. Pat the steaks bone dry, shaking off the marinade, and lay them in without crowding.
steps.tip: Wet meat will never brown, so dry them well

steps.text: Sear undisturbed until a dark crust forms and the edges look cooked partway up the side.
Flip and cook just until the second side browns, then move the steaks to a plate to rest; thin steaks go from juicy to leathery in seconds.

Dump the onions and their mojo into the hot pan, scraping up every browned bit, and cook over medium-high until they go limp and golden at the edges and the liquid reduces to a glaze. Heat the rice pouches while they cook.
Pile the onions and pan juices over the rested steaks, squeeze the last lime over the top, and serve with the beans, rice, and a scatter of cilantro.

swap: No orange? A splash of pineapple juice or an extra lime with a pinch of sugar mimics the sour orange Cubans actually use.
leftovers: Slice cold steak thin and stack it with the onions, beans, and rice in a wrap, or crisp it all together in a hot pan the next morning with a fried egg.

title: Kuku Paka: Swahili Coast Charred Chicken in Coconut Curry
blurb: Chicken blistered under the broiler and then simmered into a golden coconut sauce loaded with ginger, green chile, and lime until the whole pot tastes like the Mombasa waterfront.

ingredients.item: 4 lb Kirkwood bone-in, skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks
1 bunch cilantro, stems and leaves separated
3 Roma tomatoes, grated or finely chopped
3 cups Earthly Grains basmati rice, cooked

steps.text: Blitz the garlic, ginger, chiles, and cilantro stems with the juice of one lime and a splash of water into a rough paste. Rub half of it over the chicken along with half the turmeric and plenty of salt.
steps.tip: Let it sit while the broiler heats and the onions cook

steps.text: Heat the broiler on high and arrange the chicken skin side up on a foil-lined sheet pan. Broil until the skin is blistered, deeply charred in patches, and the fat has rendered out. It does not need to be cooked through yet.
steps.tip: Char is the whole point, so let a few spots go black

steps.text: While the chicken broils, cook the onion in olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium heat, stirring occasionally, until it is soft and just turning golden at the edges.
Add the remaining spice paste with the rest of the turmeric and the coriander and fry, stirring, until the raw garlic smell disappears and the paste darkens and tightens against the pot.
Stir in the grated tomatoes and cook them down until they go jammy and the oil separates out and slicks the surface.
Pour in both cans of coconut milk, season with salt, and bring it to a bare quiver over medium-low. Do not let it reach a rolling boil or the sauce will break.

Nestle the charred chicken and every drop of its pan juices into the sauce and simmer uncovered, spooning sauce over the tops now and then, until the meat pulls easily from the bone and the sauce coats a spoon.
Finish off the heat with the juice of another lime and most of the chopped cilantro leaves, then taste hard for salt, heat, and acid and push whichever one is lagging.
steps.tip: It should taste bright, not just rich

steps.text: Serve over the cooked basmati with the remaining cilantro and lime wedges on the side.

swap: No fresh chiles? A couple of spoonfuls of Burman's hot sauce stirred into the paste brings the heat and the vinegar edge.
leftovers: This deepens overnight and keeps for four days; pull the meat off the bones before storing so it soaks up the sauce, and thin with a splash of water when reheating gently.

title: Three-Cup Chicken with Charred Ginger and Thai Basil
blurb: Chicken chunks lacquered in a sticky sesame-soy-rice wine glaze with whole blistered garlic cloves and a whole bushel of Thai basil thrown in at the last second.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, cut in 1 1/2-inch chunks (Kirkwood)
3 tbsp Shaoxing wine or dry sherry
1 (2-inch) knob ginger, sliced into thin coins
10 garlic cloves, peeled and left whole
4 dried red chiles, snapped in half
2 packed cups Thai basil leaves, stems removed
2 bowls Trader Joe's Frozen Jasmine Rice

steps.text: Pat the chicken chunks very dry and season them with black pepper only, since the soy sauce brings all the salt this dish needs. Stir the soy sauce, wine, and brown sugar together in a small bowl so the sauce is ready to hit a hot pan.
steps.tip: Season with pepper now, salt at the very end if at all.

steps.text: Pour the sesame oil into a wok or heavy 12-inch skillet and set it over medium-low, then add the ginger coins in a single layer. Fry them gently until the edges curl, turn pale gold, and go slightly papery.
steps.tip: Low and slow here; scorched sesame oil turns bitter.

steps.text: Add the whole garlic cloves and dried chiles and keep the heat at medium-low, rolling them through the oil until the garlic is blistered and golden on two sides and the chiles darken. Fish the garlic and ginger onto a plate if they are browning faster than that.
steps.tip: Whole cloves go sweet and creamy inside.

steps.text: Crank the heat to medium-high, add the chicken in one layer, and leave it completely alone until the undersides are browned and release from the pan. Toss once and let the second side color.
steps.tip: Resist stirring or you get gray meat, not brown.

steps.text: Pour in the soy mixture, let it come to a hard bubble, then drop the heat to medium and simmer, tossing every minute or so, until the liquid reduces to a syrup that coats every chunk and pools thickly at the bottom. Heat the jasmine rice while this reduces.
steps.tip: Pull it when the glaze streaks the pan and closes slowly.

steps.text: Kill the heat, pile in the scallion batons and all the basil at once, and toss hard for a minute until the leaves collapse into the glaze and go glossy dark green. Taste and add a splash more soy if it needs it.
steps.tip: Off-heat keeps the basil perfumed instead of stewed.

steps.text: Spoon the chicken over bowls of hot jasmine rice, scraping every bit of glaze and the sweet garlic cloves out of the pan. Eat immediately while the basil is still fragrant.

swap: Out of Thai basil? Use regular basil plus an extra scallion, and add it strictly off the heat.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; the glaze sets solid when cold, so reheat in a skillet with a tablespoon of water to loosen it.

title: Poulet Provencal with Olives, Fennel and Orange
blurb: Crackling bone-in thighs roasted over burst cherry tomatoes, caramelized fennel, and briny olives, with wide strips of orange zest perfuming the whole pan.

ingredients.item: 1 large fennel bulb, cut into 1/2-inch wedges
1/2 cup pitted Kalamata or black olives
1 orange, zest peeled in wide strips plus the juice
2 tsp herbes de Provence (or Trader Joe's 21 Seasoning Salute)
1 jar Trader Joe's Quartered Marinated Artichokes, drained

steps.text: Heat the oven to 425F. Pat the thighs bone-dry, season both sides hard with salt and pepper, and set them skin side up on the counter while the oven comes up.
steps.tip: Wet skin steams; dry skin shatters.

steps.text: Film an oven-safe 10-inch skillet with olive oil over medium-high and lay the thighs in skin side down. Leave them completely untouched until the skin is deep golden and lifts cleanly from the pan when you nudge it.
steps.tip: If it sticks, it isn't ready to turn.

steps.text: Flip the thighs for one minute, then move them to a plate skin side up and pour off all but about 1 tbsp of the fat. Drop the heat to medium and lay the fennel wedges in cut side down.
Cook the fennel over medium without moving it until the flat faces are deeply caramelized and the wedges are just starting to bend. Smash the garlic and strip the orange zest while it colors.
steps.tip: Fennel goes sweet and almost meaty when browned this hard.

steps.text: Add the garlic, anchovies, crushed fennel seeds, and herbes de Provence and stir over medium until the anchovies dissolve into the fat and the pan smells like a pine forest. Pour in the wine and scrape the bottom clean.
steps.tip: The anchovy melts away completely; nobody will find it.

steps.text: Once the wine has reduced by half and lost its raw smell, stir in the tomatoes, olives, artichokes, orange zest strips, and orange juice. Nestle the thighs back in skin side up so the skin sits proud of the liquid.
steps.tip: Keep the skin above the sauce line to stay crisp.

steps.text: Slide the skillet into the oven and roast until the tomatoes burst and slump, the sauce is glossy, and the thickest thigh reads 175F. Slice and toast the baguette while it roasts.
Let the pan rest so the juices settle, then taste the sauce and adjust the salt, remembering the olives and anchovy already brought plenty. Serve straight from the skillet with bread for the sauce.
steps.tip: The orange peel is for perfume, not eating.

swap: No fennel bulb? Use two thick-sliced onions and bump the crushed fennel seeds to a full teaspoon.
leftovers: Refrigerate up to 3 days and pull the meat off the bone into the sauce; it turns into a superb pasta topper the next night.

title: Chupe de Camarones, Chilean Shrimp and Bread Chowder
blurb: A Chilean coastal classic: milk-soaked bread cooked down into a velvety smoky-red chowder, studded with sweet red shrimp and blistered under a blanket of melted cheese.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Trader Joe's Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, thawed and peeled
3 thick slices country bread, crusts torn off
2 tsp merken (or 1 1/2 tsp smoked paprika plus a pinch of cayenne)

steps.text: Tear the bread into rough pieces, drop them into a bowl with the milk, and press them under so they soak through. Meanwhile pat the shrimp dry and season them with salt and 1/2 tsp of the merken.
steps.tip: The bread is the thickener; no flour anywhere in this.

steps.text: Melt the butter in an oven-safe skillet or small Dutch oven over medium and add the onion with a big pinch of salt. Cook it slowly, stirring now and then, until it is fully soft and translucent with no browning at all.
steps.tip: Color here would muddy the clean red of the finished chowder.

steps.text: Stir in the garlic, the remaining merken, and the sweet paprika and cook over medium until the fat stains brick red and smells toasted. Do not let the paprika catch on the bottom.
steps.tip: Blooming the chiles in fat is what makes it taste Chilean.

steps.text: Scrape in the soaked bread with all its milk plus the broth, then mash and stir with a wooden spoon over medium until the bread disappears into a thick, spoon-coating porridge. Add a splash more milk if it gets stiffer than loose oatmeal.
steps.tip: Keep it moving; the bottom scorches fast.

steps.text: Stir in the cream, taste, and season aggressively with salt and pepper since the base is starchy and needs it. Turn on the broiler to high.
Drop the heat to low, nestle the shrimp into the surface of the chowder, and let them poach gently until they turn opaque and curl into loose C shapes. Do not stir them around.
steps.tip: Tight O-shaped shrimp are already overcooked.

steps.text: Scatter the mozzarella over the top and slide the pan 6 inches under the broiler until the cheese is molten with blistered brown spots.
steps.tip: Watch it the whole time; it goes from gold to black in seconds.

steps.text: Let the chowder settle so it stops volcano-bubbling, then shower it with cilantro and serve it straight from the pan with spoons.

swap: No merken anywhere? Smoked paprika plus a pinch of cayenne and a pinch of dried oregano gets you close.
leftovers: Best the day it is made, but keeps 2 days refrigerated; reheat gently with a splash of milk since the bread base tightens up cold.

title: Low-Country Shrimp and Sausage over Unexpected Cheddar Grits
blurb: A big Charleston-style skillet of shrimp, smoked sausage, and bacon in a peppery pan gravy, spooned over stone-ground grits made outrageous with Unexpected Cheddar.

ingredients.item: 2 lb Trader Joe's Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, peeled
12 oz Never Any! smoked sausage, sliced into coins
5 oz Trader Joe's Unexpected Cheddar, grated
1 bunch scallions, whites and greens sliced separately

steps.text: Bring 5 cups of the broth plus 2 cups water and 1 1/2 tsp salt to a rolling boil in a heavy pot over high heat. Rain the grits in slowly with one hand while whisking constantly with the other.
steps.tip: Whisking during the pour is the only way to avoid lumps.

steps.text: Drop the heat to the lowest simmer you can hold, cover, and cook the grits until they are creamy and no longer feel sandy on your tongue, whisking every 10 minutes and scraping the corners. Prep everything else while they cook.
steps.tip: Taste, do not time; sandy grits are undercooked grits.

steps.text: Put the bacon in a large cold skillet and set it over medium so the fat renders out slowly. Cook until the pieces are crisp and the pan holds a generous slick of fat, then lift the bacon out to a paper towel and leave the fat behind.
steps.tip: Starting cold renders more fat and burns less.

steps.text: Raise the heat to medium-high and lay the sausage coins in the bacon fat in one layer. Sear without stirring until the cut faces are caramelized and the edges cup upward, then push them to one side.

Add the bell pepper and scallion whites and cook over medium-high until softened with charred edges, stirring in the garlic for the last minute so it perfumes without burning. Season the shrimp with salt and pepper while this happens.
steps.tip: Garlic goes in last; it burns in half the time peppers need.

steps.text: Add the shrimp in a single layer and leave them undisturbed until the undersides turn pink, then toss and cook just until opaque through and curled. Pull the pan off the heat immediately.
steps.tip: They will keep cooking in the hot gravy, so undershoot.

steps.text: Stir the hot sauce, the juice of the whole lemon, the remaining 1 cup broth, and half the bacon into the skillet, scraping the browned bits loose into what is now a loose, peppery pan gravy. Taste for salt.
steps.tip: The broth plus fond is the gravy; nothing else needed.

steps.text: Kill the heat under the grits and beat in the butter and Unexpected Cheddar until glossy and pourable, adding a splash of water if they have gone stiff. Season with salt and plenty of black pepper.
steps.tip: Off the heat so the cheese emulsifies instead of breaking.

steps.text: Ladle the grits into wide bowls, spoon the shrimp and sausage with all their gravy over the top, and finish with the remaining bacon and the scallion greens.

swap: Can't find stone-ground grits? Use coarse yellow polenta and cut the covered cooking time to 20 minutes.
leftovers: Store the grits and the shrimp mixture in separate containers for up to 3 days; loosen the grits with milk over low heat and warm the shrimp only briefly so they don't turn rubbery.

title: Nepali Chicken Chhoila with Mustard Oil and Timur
blurb: Blackened chicken hacked into chunks and doused in smoking mustard oil bloomed with red chile, fenugreek, and tongue-tingling timur pepper.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs (Simply Nature Organic)
1 (2-inch) knob ginger and 4 garlic cloves, grated to a paste

steps.text: Toast the timur and fenugreek seeds in a dry skillet over medium, shaking constantly, until they smell nutty and the fenugreek darkens one shade. Crush them coarsely in a mortar or under a heavy pan and set aside.
steps.tip: Fenugreek turns bitter the second it goes past golden brown.

steps.text: Pat the thighs completely dry and rub them with the ginger-garlic paste, the turmeric, half the ground chili, and a heavy pinch of salt. Set a cast iron skillet over medium-high until it smokes faintly.
Lay the thighs down with just a slick of oil and leave them absolutely still until the undersides are blackened in patches and the meat releases from the pan on its own.
steps.tip: You want real char, not color; this is a grill dish indoors.

steps.text: Flip and cook the second side until the thickest part reads 175F and the juices run clear. Sliver the onion and chop the cilantro while it finishes.
Rest the chicken on a board, then hack it into rough 3/4-inch cubes, blackened edges and all, and pile it into a large bowl with the onion and cilantro.
steps.tip: Resting first keeps the juices in the bowl, not on the board.

steps.text: Heat the mustard oil in a small pan over medium-high until it shimmers and smells sharp and pungent, then add the dried chiles, the remaining ground chili, and the crushed timur-fenugreek. Swirl until it foams and turns dark red.
steps.tip: Mustard oil must be heated to smoking to lose its raw bite.

steps.text: Pour the sizzling oil straight over the chicken so it crackles, add the juice of the whole lemon and a good pinch of salt, and toss hard until every cube is stained red and slick. Taste and push the salt and lemon further than feels polite.
steps.tip: Chhoila should be loud, sour, and salty.

steps.text: Warm the naan directly in the hot dry skillet over medium-high until puffed and spotted on both sides, then serve alongside the chicken.

swap: No mustard oil? Use neutral oil with 1 tsp dry mustard powder whisked in, and heat it the same way.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and is meant to be eaten cold or at room temperature, so pack it straight into lunch containers.

title: Pasta con le Sarde, Sicilian Sardines with Fennel and Saffron
blurb: The great Palermo street dish: sardines melted into a saffron-stained fennel sauce with plumped raisins, toasted pine nuts, and a snowdrift of crunchy breadcrumbs instead of cheese.

ingredients.item: 3 tins sardines packed in olive oil, drained
1 large fennel bulb with fronds, bulb diced and fronds chopped
1/4 cup Southern Grove pine nuts or slivered almonds

steps.text: Bring a large pot of aggressively salted water to a boil over high heat. Crumble the saffron into 1/3 cup of very hot water in a mug and drop the raisins in to steep and plump.
steps.tip: Blooming saffron in hot water pulls out far more color.

steps.text: Toast the breadcrumbs with 1 tbsp olive oil in a dry skillet over medium, stirring nonstop, until they are sandy gold and audibly crisp. Scrape them onto a plate.
steps.tip: These are the Sicilian answer to parmesan; do not skip them.

steps.text: Add the pine nuts to the same pan over medium and toast until freckled brown, then tip them out with the breadcrumbs.
steps.tip: Pull them early; they scorch off residual heat.

steps.text: Add a generous glug of olive oil to the pan, raise to medium-high, and cook the diced fennel and onion with a pinch of salt until softened and browning at the edges. Drop the pasta into the boiling water as soon as they go in.
steps.tip: Slightly browned fennel is sweeter than pale fennel.

steps.text: Stir in the anchovies, tomato paste, and red pepper flakes and mash them into the vegetables over medium until the anchovies dissolve and the paste darkens from red to brick.

Pour in the saffron water with the raisins plus a ladle of pasta water and simmer over medium until it looks like a loose, golden-orange sauce. Break two tins of sardines into big flakes and fold them in gently so some pieces stay whole.
steps.tip: Fold, don't stir, or the sardines turn to paste.

steps.text: Drain the pasta one minute shy of al dente and drop it straight into the pan with another splash of pasta water. Toss over medium-high until the sauce clings to every strand and the pasta is just al dente.
steps.tip: Starchy pasta water is what makes it cling.

steps.text: Off the heat, squeeze in half the lemon, taste for salt, and pile it into bowls. Top with the reserved tin of sardines, the fennel fronds, and a heavy shower of breadcrumbs and pine nuts.

swap: No sardines on the shelf? Two tins of Northern Catch tuna in oil work, folded in at the very end so they stay chunky.
leftovers: Keeps 2 days refrigerated; store the breadcrumbs separately at room temperature and re-toast them briefly so the topping stays crunchy.

title: Trinidadian Brown Stew Chicken with Burnt Sugar
blurb: Chicken caramelized in a pot of scorched brown sugar until it turns mahogany, then simmered down with green seasoning and a whole scotch bonnet into a glossy, slightly bitter-sweet gravy.

ingredients.item: 1 1/2 lb bone-in skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks (Kirkwood)
1 bunch cilantro and 4 scallions, roughly chopped together

steps.text: Chop the cilantro, scallions, garlic, thyme, and half the scotch bonnet together into a rough wet paste with 2 tbsp water, or pulse it in a small food processor. Rub two-thirds of this green seasoning and 1 tsp salt all over the chicken and leave it to sit while you prep the rest.
steps.tip: Green seasoning is the backbone of every Trini pot.

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a heavy pot over medium, add the brown sugar, and let it melt mostly undisturbed until it darkens to the color of dark molasses, foams, and starts to smoke faintly. Pull it one shade before you think you should.
steps.tip: This burnt sugar is the whole dish; black and acrid means start over.

steps.text: Scrape the marinade off the chicken and reserve it, then lower the pieces into the bubbling caramel skin side down; they will hiss and seize. Turn them with tongs over medium heat until every side is coated deep mahogany.
steps.tip: Wet marinade in hot caramel will spatter, so use tongs and stand back.

steps.text: Add the onion and bell pepper and cook over medium until they slump and pick up the dark color from the pot, scraping the bottom as they release moisture.
Stir in the reserved green seasoning, soy sauce, ketchup, broth, and the remaining scotch bonnet half left whole. Scrape the bottom of the pot completely clean and bring it to a simmer.
steps.tip: Whole chile in the pot gives fruity perfume without much burn.

steps.text: Cover, drop to low, and simmer until the chicken pulls easily from the bone with a fork. Heat the rice pouches during the last few minutes.
steps.tip: A bare blip, not a boil, or the meat tightens up.

steps.text: Uncover, fish out the chile, raise the heat to medium-high, and reduce the gravy until it turns glossy and coats the back of a spoon. Spoon it over the chicken as it thickens.
Taste for salt, remembering the soy sauce, and serve the chicken over jasmine rice with the gravy poured generously over everything.

swap: No scotch bonnet? Use a habanero, or 1 tbsp Burman's hot sauce stirred in with the broth.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and the gravy deepens overnight; reheat covered over low with a splash of broth.

title: Kashmiri Rogan Josh with Fennel and Black Cardamom
blurb: Lamb braised low in a yogurt gravy stained brilliant red with Kashmiri chile and scented with ground fennel, dry ginger, and smoky black cardamom, finished when a slick of spiced oil rises to the top.

ingredients.item: 3 lb boneless lamb shoulder, cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes
1 1/2 cups Friendly Farms whole-milk Greek yogurt, whisked smooth
4 black cardamom pods, 6 green cardamom pods, 1 cinnamon stick and 6 cloves
3 pouches Journey to India basmati rice

steps.text: Pat the lamb cubes very dry and season them with salt. Melt the ghee in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until it shimmers, then add the whole spices and bay leaves and fry until the cardamom pods puff and the kitchen smells like a spice shop.
steps.tip: Whole spices go in first so the fat carries their perfume everywhere.

steps.text: Add half the lamb in a single uncrowded layer and sear over medium-high, undisturbed, until the underside is deep brown and lifts cleanly, then turn to brown a second face. Transfer to a bowl and repeat with the rest.
steps.tip: Two batches; crowded lamb steams gray and never browns.

steps.text: Drop the heat to medium-low and sprinkle the asafoetida into the fat for a few seconds, then whisk in the Kashmiri chili powder along with 1/4 cup water so it turns into a glossy red paste instead of scorching.
steps.tip: The splash of water is what keeps the chile from burning bitter.

steps.text: Pull the pot off the burner for a moment, then stir in the whisked yogurt a few spoonfuls at a time, stirring constantly between additions, until the sauce is smooth and uniformly brick red.
steps.tip: Adding it cold or all at once will split the yogurt into curds.

steps.text: Return the lamb and every drop of its juices to the pot, then stir in the ground fennel, dry ginger, 2 tsp salt, and 2 cups water. Bring it back to a lazy simmer over medium.
Cover and hold it at the barest simmer, stirring and scraping the bottom every 10 minutes so the yogurt doesn't catch. The surface should blip occasionally, never roll.
steps.tip: If it is bubbling hard, your low is too high.

steps.text: Uncover, raise to medium-low, and simmer until the lamb is fork-tender and the gravy has reduced to a thick rust-red sauce with a distinct slick of red oil pooling on the surface. That rising oil is the classic sign it is done.
steps.tip: Skim the oil or stir it back in, cook's choice.

steps.text: Stir in the garam masala off the heat, taste for salt, and let the pot rest while you heat the rice pouches and warm the naan in a dry skillet over medium-high.
steps.tip: Garam masala goes in at the end so it stays fragrant.

steps.text: Fish out the cinnamon stick and the black cardamom pods, then ladle the lamb over basmati in wide bowls with naan on the side.
steps.tip: Black cardamom pods are not for eating whole.

swap: No lamb shoulder? Use 3 lb bone-in chicken thighs and cut the covered simmer to 20 minutes.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes for 3 months; the flavor deepens noticeably by day two.

title: Singapore Chili Shrimp with Egg Ribbon Gravy
blurb: Sweet, sour and fiery tomato-chili gravy shot through with silky egg ribbons, piled with plump red shrimp and torn naan for mopping the pan clean.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, peeled and thawed
1 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
4 scallions, thinly sliced on an angle
2 tsp cornstarch stirred into 2 tbsp cold water

steps.text: Pat the shrimp completely dry and season them lightly with salt, then spread them on a plate so they are not touching. Leave them out while you build the sauce so they lose their fridge chill.
steps.tip: Dry shrimp sear instead of steam.

steps.text: Stir the sweet chili sauce, ketchup, sriracha, soy sauce and 1/2 cup water together in a bowl until smooth. Slice the scallions and grate the garlic and ginger while you are at the board.
Heat a wide skillet over medium-high with a slick of olive oil, then add the garlic and ginger. Stir constantly until they smell sweet and the garlic just turns pale gold at the edges.
steps.tip: Do not let the garlic brown.

steps.text: Pour in the sauce mixture and bring it to a hard bubble. Simmer, stirring now and then, until it darkens from orange to brick red and coats the back of a spoon.

Slide the shrimp in one layer and cook, flipping once, until they curl into loose C-shapes and turn opaque all the way through. Red shrimp go fast, so pull them the moment the last gray streak disappears.
steps.tip: A tight O means overcooked.

steps.text: Stir the cornstarch slurry and drizzle it in, swirling the pan until the gravy turns glossy. Then pour the beaten egg in a thin stream across the surface, wait without stirring until it sets into ribbons, and fold it in gently.
While the gravy finishes, toast the naan in a dry skillet or directly over a gas flame until it puffs and picks up blistered black spots. Tear it into big mopping pieces.
Shower the shrimp with scallions and squeeze a lime wedge over the whole pan. Serve straight from the skillet with the charred naan alongside.

swap: If the Argentinian red shrimp are out, any large raw frozen shrimp works, but cut the cooking time down since they are leaner and firm up faster.
leftovers: Refrigerate shrimp and gravy together for up to two days and reheat gently with a splash of water, then spoon over hot rice.

title: Mustard-Dill Salmon with Smashed Dill Potatoes
blurb: Crisp-skinned salmon under a sweet-sharp mustard and dill sauce, with buttery smashed potatoes and cold vinegared cucumber for contrast.

ingredients.item: 1 Persian cucumber, shaved into thin coins

steps.text: Cover the potatoes with heavily salted cold water, bring to a boil, and cook until a paring knife slides into the biggest one with zero resistance. Start the sauce while they bubble away.
steps.tip: Salt the water like the sea.

steps.text: Whisk both mustards, the honey and the vinegar into a thick, mayonnaise-glossy sauce, then fold in a large handful of chopped dill. Let it sit so the mustard mellows.
Toss the cucumber coins with a pinch of salt and a splash more vinegar and slide them into the fridge to crisp and turn translucent at the edges.

Pat the salmon bone-dry and season both sides. Heat olive oil in a skillet over medium-high until it shimmers and thins, then lay the fillets in skin-down and press each flat with a spatula for a few seconds.
steps.tip: Pressing stops the skin curling.

steps.text: Cook undisturbed until the skin releases cleanly from the pan and the flesh turns pale and opaque two-thirds of the way up the sides.
Flip and cook just until the center gives softly when pressed, then move the fillets to plates skin-side up so the crust stays crackly.
Drain the potatoes and return them to the hot dry pot, then crush each one flat with the back of a spoon and toss with the butter, the capers and more chopped dill until glossy.
Dollop the yogurt over the potatoes, spoon the mustard-dill sauce generously over the salmon, and serve with the cold cucumbers and a lemon wedge.

swap: No fresh dill in the store? Use a big handful of chopped fresh parsley plus a teaspoon of dried dill stirred into the sauce early so it can soften.
leftovers: Flake cold salmon into the leftover potatoes with an extra spoonful of the mustard sauce for a Nordic-style salad the next day.

title: Salvadoran Panes con Pollo
blurb: Chicken braised into a toasted-seed relajo tomato sauce, heaped onto buttery toasted buns with crunchy vinegared cabbage and cold radish.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Kirkwood boneless skinless chicken thighs

steps.text: Toast the pepitas and sesame seeds in a dry skillet over medium, shaking often, until they pop and turn nut-brown and fragrant. Tip them onto a board and chop them fine, or crush them with the bottom of a mug.
steps.tip: This crushed seed paste is the relajo.

steps.text: Season the chicken thighs hard with salt and pepper. Add olive oil to the same skillet over medium-high and sear the thighs undisturbed until the undersides are deep mahogany.
Flip the chicken, add the onion and garlic around it, and cook until the onion slumps and starts to take color in the rendered fat.
Pour in the tomato sauce, the crushed seeds, the oregano, the cumin and 1/2 cup water. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook at a lazy bubble until the chicken pulls apart under a fork.
While the chicken braises, toss the cabbage and radishes with a big pinch of salt and a splash of vinegar or lime, then press it down in the bowl and leave it to wilt and sharpen.
Shred the chicken directly in the pan with two forks, then simmer uncovered until the sauce thickens enough to cling to the meat rather than run off it.
steps.tip: You want it saucy, not soupy.

steps.text: Split the brioche buns, spread the cut sides with mayonnaise, and toast them face-down in a dry skillet over medium until the edges are crisp and freckled brown.
Pile the chicken onto the bottom buns, spoon extra sauce over so it soaks in, and crown with a tangle of the cabbage and radish before closing the sandwiches.

swap: No brioche buns left? Any soft roll or even folded Naan holds up, as long as you toast the cut side so the sauce does not turn it to mush.
leftovers: Store the saucy chicken on its own for up to three days and rebuild the sandwiches fresh, toasting new buns so they stay crisp.

title: Goan Pork Vindaloo
blurb: Pork shoulder braised in a vinegar-and-chili paste until the sauce turns dark, glossy and fierce, with just enough sweetness to keep the heat honest.

ingredients.item: 3 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 1 1/2-inch cubes

steps.text: Whisk the vinegar, garlic, ginger, paprika, cumin, garam masala, turmeric, cayenne, brown sugar and a heavy pinch of salt into a loose rust-red paste. Toss the pork through it until every cube is coated and leave it to marinate while you chop the onion.
steps.tip: Vinegar first is what makes it vindaloo.

steps.text: Heat a film of olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high until it ripples. Lift the pork out of the marinade, letting the excess drip back into the bowl, and brown it in two uncrowded batches until each side is deeply crusted.
steps.tip: Crowding steams the meat.

steps.text: Set the pork aside and drop the heat to medium. Add the onion and cook, scraping the browned bits off the bottom, until it is soft and the edges are golden.
Return the pork and every drop of the reserved marinade to the pot, pour in 1 cup water, and bring it to a strong bubble while you scrape the base clean one last time.
Cover, lower the heat until the surface just shivers, and simmer until the pork surrenders to a fork with no resistance. Stir once halfway to keep the bottom from catching.
While it simmers, heat the rice pouches and fluff them into a wide bowl with a fork so the grains stay separate.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium, and reduce until the sauce clings to the pork and a slick of red-tinted oil rises to the surface.
steps.tip: The oil surfacing means it is done.

steps.text: Pull the pot off the heat and let it settle, then taste and adjust with salt or another splash of vinegar for brightness before spooning it over the basmati.

swap: Pork shoulder unavailable? Bone-in chicken thighs work with the same paste, but cut the covered simmer down so the meat does not fall to threads.
leftovers: Vindaloo is better on day two once the vinegar mellows, so refrigerate up to four days or freeze in portions and reheat with a splash of water.

title: Chicken Kyiv Cutlets with Garlic-Dill Butter
blurb: Shatteringly crisp golden cutlets that leak a river of garlicky dill butter the moment your knife goes in, with dill peas and mustardy smetana alongside.

ingredients.item: 1 cup neutral oil, for shallow frying

steps.text: Mash the softened butter with the garlic, a fistful of chopped dill, salt and pepper. Roll it into two tight logs in plastic wrap and freeze until hard to the touch.
steps.tip: Rock-hard butter will not leak out while frying.

steps.text: Butterfly each breast almost in half and open it like a book, then pound it between two sheets of plastic until it is an even thin sheet with no thick lump in the middle.
Lay a frozen butter log on each cutlet, fold the sides in, and roll it up into a tight parcel, pressing the seam and ends firmly closed so there is no gap.
steps.tip: Any gap is an escape route.

steps.text: Set out flour, beaten egg and breadcrumbs in three dishes. Roll each parcel through flour, then egg, then crumbs, then egg and crumbs a second time, pressing hard for a thick armored coating. Chill the breaded rolls while the oil heats.

Heat about half an inch of oil in a deep skillet over medium until a dropped breadcrumb sizzles steadily on contact. Lower the rolls in seam-side down and fry, turning every couple of minutes, until every side is deep even gold.
Move the cutlets to a rack set over a sheet pan and finish them in a 400F oven until the thickest part is firm and springy rather than squishy.
While they finish, simmer the peas in salted water until bright green and just tender, then drain and toss them with chopped dill and a squeeze of lemon.
Stir the sour cream with the mustard, a spoonful of lemon juice and more dill until it is pourable, and season it sharply.
Rest the cutlets briefly so the butter stops boiling inside, then cut into them at the table and let the garlic butter flood the plate.
steps.tip: Cut at the table for the reveal.

swap: If chicken breasts look thin and ragged, use two large boneless thighs pounded flat instead; they roll even more forgivingly around the butter.
leftovers: Refrigerate cutlets uncovered on a rack and re-crisp them in a hot oven, never the microwave, which turns the crust to paste.

title: Hawaij Chicken with Sahawiq and Charred Naan
blurb: Peppery, cardamom-scented chicken seared to a mahogany crust and slathered with sahawiq, the raw green chili-cilantro relish that lights the whole plate up.

ingredients.item: 1 1/2 lb Never Any! boneless skinless chicken thighs

steps.text: Whisk the cumin, coriander, turmeric, cardamom, a very generous grind of black pepper, salt, two grated garlic cloves and olive oil into a thick hawaij rub. Massage it into the thighs and leave them out while the pan heats.
steps.tip: Black pepper is the backbone of hawaij.

steps.text: Heat a cast iron skillet over medium-high until a drop of water skitters instantly. Lay the thighs in smooth-side down and leave them completely alone so the spices toast into a crust.
Flip the chicken when the undersides are dark mahogany and cook until the thickest piece is firm and the juices run clear.

While the chicken sears, make the sahawiq: chop the cilantro, chilies, remaining garlic and tomatoes together on a board until you have a rough, wet green-flecked relish, then season it hard with salt and lemon juice.
steps.tip: Chop, do not puree, for texture.

steps.text: Move the chicken to a board to rest, and while it does, press the naan into the spiced drippings in the hot pan until it puffs and the edges blacken in spots.
Stir the lemon zest and a pinch of salt into the yogurt so it tastes bright rather than flat.
Slice the chicken thickly against the grain, pile it onto the charred naan, and spoon over the sahawiq and cold yogurt just before eating.

swap: Out of fresh chilies? A spoonful of Green Dragon Hot Sauce stirred into the chopped cilantro and tomato gets you close to the same raw green heat.
leftovers: Keep the sahawiq in a jar under a thin film of olive oil for up to five days and spoon it over eggs, rice or the leftover sliced chicken.

title: Tuscan Rosemary Pork Chops with Cannellini and Kale
blurb: Thick chops basted in foaming rosemary-sage oil, served over creamy smashed cannellini beans with kale wilted right into the pan drippings.

ingredients.item: 2 bone-in pork chops, about 1 inch thick
1 bunch lacinato kale, stripped and torn

steps.text: Salt the chops aggressively on both sides and let them sit on the counter while you strip the kale and smash the garlic, so they lose their chill and the salt sinks in.
steps.tip: Room-temperature chops cook evenly.

steps.text: Heat a heavy skillet over medium-high with the olive oil until it shimmers and sends up a first wisp of smoke. Lay the chops in away from you and do not touch them until a hard dark crust forms underneath.

Flip the chops and add the rosemary, sage and half the garlic to the pan. Tilt the skillet and spoon the sizzling herb oil over the meat continuously until the chops feel firm with a slight give near the bone.
steps.tip: Basting is what perfumes the meat.

steps.text: Move the chops to a board with the crisped herbs on top and let them rest while you build the beans in the same pan.
Lower the heat to medium and add the remaining garlic and the red pepper flakes to the drippings, stirring until they sizzle steadily and smell sweet.
Add the beans and the broth, then crush about a third of the beans against the side of the pan. Simmer until the liquid turns creamy and coats the whole spoon.
Fold in the kale by the handful and cook until it collapses into glossy dark green ribbons and the pan is nearly dry again.
Finish the beans with lemon juice and the parmesan, then spoon them onto plates, set the chops on top, and zigzag the balsamic glaze over everything.

swap: No lacinato kale? Baby spinach or Swiss chard wilts into the beans just as well, though it needs barely a minute in the pan.
leftovers: Slice the cold chops thin and stir them into the beans with extra broth for a next-day Tuscan bean soup.

title: Puerto Rican Carne Guisada with Olives and Potatoes
blurb: Beef stewed down into a deep sofrito-and-tomato gravy studded with briny olives and potatoes that drink up every bit of it.

ingredients.item: 2 1/2 lb beef chuck, cut into 3/4-inch cubes
1 green bell pepper, seeded and torn

steps.text: Pat the beef dry and season it hard with salt, pepper and half the oregano. Heat olive oil in a Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the cubes in two uncrowded batches until they are crusted on at least two sides.
steps.tip: Small cubes turn tender inside the short simmer.

steps.text: While the beef browns, pulse the onion, bell pepper, garlic and the cilantro stems in a food processor, or chop them very fine by hand, into a rough wet sofrito.

Lift the beef out, drop the heat to medium, and add the sofrito to the drippings. Cook, scraping the fond up off the bottom, until the raw onion smell is gone and the mixture looks jammy rather than watery.
Stir in the paprika and the remaining oregano for a few seconds, then add the tomato sauce and cook until it darkens to brick red and pulls away from the pan when you drag a spoon through.
Return the beef and its juices, pour in the broth, and bring it to a bubble. Cover, drop the heat until the surface barely shivers, and simmer.
Add the potatoes and olives, pushing them under the liquid, then cover again and simmer until the potatoes are fork-tender and the beef pulls apart under light pressure.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium, and reduce until the gravy thickly coats a spoon and the potatoes sit half-submerged instead of swimming.
steps.tip: Some potato will break down and thicken it for you.

steps.text: While it reduces, heat the rice pouches and fluff them so the grains separate.
Pull the pot off the heat, stir in a big handful of chopped cilantro leaves, and let it settle before ladling it over the rice.

swap: No beef chuck in the case? Boneless country-style pork ribs cut the same size work beautifully and turn tender in about the same time.
leftovers: The gravy tightens overnight, so refrigerate up to four days and loosen with broth when reheating, or spoon it into warm tortillas for lunch.

title: Shanghai Red-Braised Chicken with Star Anise and Scallions
blurb: Mahogany-glazed thighs simmered in soy, brown sugar and star anise until the sauce turns to lacquer and clings to every piece.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs, halved
3 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
6 scallions, cut into 2-inch lengths, whites and greens separated
2 heads baby bok choy, halved lengthwise

steps.text: Pat the chicken thoroughly dry. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide skillet over medium-high until it shimmers and thins out, then lay the thighs in a single layer and sear undisturbed until the undersides are deep golden and release from the pan without tugging.
steps.tip: Crowding steams the meat instead of browning it.

steps.text: Push the chicken to one side and drop the ginger coins, smashed garlic and scallion whites into the bare patch. Stir them in the hot fat until they smell sweet and toasty and the garlic edges turn pale gold.
Pour in the soy sauce, sherry and brown sugar along with 1/2 cup water, then drop in the star anise. Scrape the browned bits off the bottom and bring everything to a hard, rolling bubble.
Lower the heat to medium-low, cover, and simmer until the chicken is fork-tender and the liquid has reduced by about half. Turn the pieces once halfway through so both sides take on color.
steps.tip: A lazy blip-blip bubble, not a boil.

steps.text: Nestle the bok choy halves cut-side down into the braising liquid and re-cover. Cook until the stems are crisp-tender and the leaves have collapsed and gone glossy dark green.
While the bok choy steams, heat the frozen jasmine rice according to the bag and fluff it with a fork.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, and boil the sauce down, spooning it over the chicken, until it is syrupy and coats the back of a spoon in a thin sheet.
steps.tip: It thickens further off the heat, so pull it a touch loose.

steps.text: Kill the heat and swirl in the rice vinegar and sesame oil. Fish out the star anise, pile the chicken and bok choy over the rice, and shower with the raw scallion greens.

swap: No dry sherry on hand — use an equal amount of unsweetened apple juice plus an extra splash of rice vinegar.
leftovers: Refrigerate the chicken sitting in its sauce for up to three days; the glaze sets to a jelly cold and re-melts perfectly over fresh rice.

title: Bengali Shorshe Salmon in Mustard-Turmeric Sauce
blurb: Salmon poached in a sharp, sinus-clearing mustard gravy stained gold with turmeric and punctuated by crackling nigella seeds and slit green chiles.

ingredients.item: 1 tbsp Burman's stone-ground or Dijon mustard
3 tbsp mustard oil or other neutral oil

steps.text: Rub the salmon all over with the turmeric and a generous pinch of salt and set it aside while you build the sauce.
steps.tip: The turmeric seasons the fish and stains it a deep marigold.

steps.text: Whisk both mustards with the sugar and 3/4 cup water until completely smooth and pourable, with no thick paste clinging to the whisk.

Heat the mustard oil in a lidded skillet over medium-high until it just begins to wisp smoke, then cut the heat to medium and add the nigella seeds and slit chiles. They should crackle and sputter the instant they hit the oil.
steps.tip: Smoking the oil first burns off its raw pungency.

steps.text: Pour in the mustard slurry, stand back from the fumes, and simmer until it loses its raw bite and thickens just enough to leave a trail behind the spoon.
Slide the salmon in, spoon sauce over the top, cover, and poach over medium-low until the fish flakes when nudged at the thickest part and the center has just turned matte.
While the fish poaches, heat the basmati pouch and tear the cilantro.

Take the pan off the heat, squeeze in half the lime, and let it stand uncovered so the sauce tightens around the fish. Serve over the rice with cilantro, the softened chiles, and the rest of the lime.

swap: No fresh serranos — stir a teaspoon of Green Dragon Hot Sauce into the sauce right at the end.
leftovers: Keep the fish and sauce together for up to two days and rewarm gently over low heat, since a hard boil turns the mustard bitter.

title: Catalan Romesco Shrimp with Blistered Scallions
blurb: Sweet red shrimp seared hard and dragged through a smoky almond-and-roasted-pepper romesco, with charred scallions for scooping.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, thawed and patted dry
1 bag Fire Roasted Peppers & Onions, thawed and drained

steps.text: Warm 3 tbsp olive oil in a skillet over medium and fry one slice of bread, torn into rough pieces, together with the whole garlic cloves until both are golden brown and crisp at the edges.
steps.tip: Fried bread is what gives romesco its body.

steps.text: Scrape the bread and garlic into a food processor with the almonds, drained fire roasted peppers and onions, smoked paprika, sherry vinegar and crushed red pepper. Blitz to a coarse, spoonable sauce with visible flecks of almond, then season with salt.
Wipe the skillet, set it over high heat, and lay the scallions in a single layer. Leave them alone until they blister and blacken in spots, then turn once and char the other side.
steps.tip: You want real black patches, not gentle browning.

steps.text: While the scallions char, pat the shrimp dry a second time and season them with salt.
steps.tip: Wet shrimp steam and turn rubbery.

steps.text: Pile the scallions onto a platter. Add a slick of oil to the ripping-hot pan and lay the shrimp down in one layer, searing undisturbed until the edges turn opaque pink and the bottoms curl.
Flip and cook just until the shrimp are opaque through the middle and springy to the touch.
steps.tip: Argentinian reds cook fast; pull them early.

steps.text: Toast the remaining bread slice, squeeze lemon over the shrimp, and spoon a thick bed of romesco onto each plate. Drag the shrimp and scallions through it and finish with parsley.

swap: Out of Argentinian reds? Any large raw shrimp works, or sear chicken tenders and slice them over the same sauce.
leftovers: Romesco keeps a week in the fridge under a slick of olive oil and is excellent on fried eggs or roast chicken.

title: Venezuelan Pabellon Bowls with Sweet Plantains
blurb: Cumin-scented beef guiso, brothy black beans and caramelized sweet plantains piled over rice with a snowfall of salty white cheese.

ingredients.item: 2 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
4 oz Happy Farms queso fresco or feta, crumbled

steps.text: Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in your largest pot over medium-high. Add the onion, bell pepper and a big pinch of salt and cook, stirring now and then, until the vegetables slump completely and the edges catch brown.
steps.tip: This sofrito is the backbone of the dish, so let it go past merely soft.

steps.text: Push the sofrito to the rim, add the beef in the center, press it into a flat slab, and leave it untouched so it browns hard before you break it into crumbles.
Stir in the garlic, cumin and oregano and cook until the spices coat the meat and smell toasted rather than dusty.
Add the tomatoes and Worcestershire, scrape the bottom clean, and simmer uncovered, stirring every few minutes, until the guiso is thick and glossy with no watery pool at the edges.

While the beef simmers, heat the oven to 425F and tip the black beans with all their liquid into a saucepan. Season with salt and a pinch of cumin and simmer until brothy but slightly thickened, smashing a few beans against the side of the pot.
steps.tip: Those smashed beans give the pot body.

steps.text: Spread the frozen plantains on a sheet pan and roast, turning once, until the edges are dark, sticky and caramelized.
Heat the rice pouches in the last few minutes and fluff them into a serving bowl.
Build each bowl in stripes: rice, then guiso, then brothy beans, then plantains, and crumble the queso fresco over the top.

swap: No frozen sweet plantains — halve two very ripe bananas lengthwise and pan-fry them in butter until deeply caramelized.
leftovers: Store the guiso, beans and plantains separately for up to four days; the beef also makes a terrific filling for arepas or tacos.

title: Isan Pork Larb with Toasted Rice Powder
blurb: Fiery lime-soaked minced pork tossed with fistfuls of mint and nutty toasted rice powder, scooped up with ice-cold cabbage leaves.

ingredients.item: 2 tbsp uncooked jasmine or basmati rice
1 tbsp Thai chili flakes or crushed red pepper

steps.text: Toast the raw rice in a dry skillet over medium, shaking the pan constantly, until every grain is the color of weak tea and the kitchen smells like popcorn.
steps.tip: This powder is the soul of larb, so do not skip it.

steps.text: Grind the toasted rice to a coarse sand in a mortar, spice grinder, or a zip-top bag under a rolling pin, then set it aside.
Add 1/4 cup water to the same skillet over medium-high, drop in the pork, and mash it into fine crumbles with the back of a spoon. Cook until no pink remains but the meat still looks moist and loose.
steps.tip: The splash of water keeps the pork tender instead of crusty.

steps.text: While the pork cooks, slice the shallot and scallions, pick the mint leaves, and separate the cabbage leaves into a bowl of ice water so they go glassy and crisp.
Kill the heat and pour in the fish sauce, lime juice, sugar and chili flakes. Stir and taste: it should be aggressively sour, salty and hot, all at once.
steps.tip: Season while the pork is warm so it drinks the dressing in.

steps.text: Fold in the shallot, scallions, most of the herbs and all but a spoonful of the rice powder. The mixture should look glossy and clumped, never soupy.
Pile the larb into a bowl, dust with the reserved rice powder and remaining herbs, and serve with the drained cabbage leaves and hot jasmine rice.

swap: Ground chicken or turkey stands in for pork; add an extra splash of fish sauce to make up for the leaner meat.
