leftovers: Larb keeps two days cold and is arguably better straight from the fridge, stuffed into lettuce cups or protein wraps.

title: Danish Frikadeller with Dill Potatoes and Agurkesalat
blurb: Butter-fried pork-and-beef patties perfumed with allspice, served with dill-slicked potatoes and sweet-sour paper-thin cucumbers.

ingredients.item: 1/2 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
1 small onion, grated on a box grater

steps.text: Put the potatoes in a pot of cold salted water, bring to a boil over high heat, then cook at a steady simmer until a knife slides into the largest one with no resistance.
While the potatoes cook, toss the cucumber slices with the vinegar, sugar and 1/2 tsp salt and refrigerate. They will go limp and translucent and release a pool of sharp brine.

Grate the onion straight into a bowl, juice and all, then add the pork, beef, egg, flour, allspice, 1 1/2 tsp salt and plenty of pepper. Beat hard with a wooden spoon until the mass turns pale, sticky and springy.
steps.tip: The beating is what gives frikadeller their bounce.

steps.text: Melt 3 tbsp of the butter in a large skillet over medium until it foams. Scoop the meat with a spoon, shape ovals with a wet hand, and set them straight into the foaming butter.
steps.tip: Wet hands keep the mixture from gluing itself to you.

steps.text: Fry undisturbed until the undersides are deep mahogany and a spatula lifts them cleanly.
steps.tip: Keep it at medium; butter scorches above that.

steps.text: Flip and fry the second side until browned and firm when pressed, with no pink at the center of the thickest one.
Drain the potatoes, return them to the hot dry pot, add the remaining butter and most of the dill, and swirl the pot until every potato glistens and a few skins split.
Plate the frikadeller with the dill potatoes and a drained mound of the cucumber salad, then spoon the browned butter from the skillet over the top.

swap: All pork or all beef works fine; with a leaner blend, beat a splash of milk into the mixture to keep the patties juicy.
leftovers: Cold frikadeller are a Danish lunchbox staple — slice them onto rye bread with mustard and the leftover pickled cucumber.

title: Guatemalan Pollo en Jocon
blurb: Chicken simmered in a vivid green tomatillo and cilantro sauce thickened the old way, with toasted pumpkin and sesame seeds.

ingredients.item: 1 (16 oz) jar Casa Mamita salsa verde
1 bunch cilantro, leaves and tender stems

steps.text: Toast the pepitas and sesame seeds together in a dry skillet over medium, shaking often, until the pepitas puff and pop and the sesame turns gold.
steps.tip: Pull them the moment they smell nutty; they scorch in seconds.

steps.text: Blend the toasted seeds with the salsa verde, cilantro, scallions, bell pepper, garlic and coriander until completely smooth and shockingly bright green.
Season the chicken thighs generously with salt. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wide pot over medium-high and sear them in a single layer until the undersides are well browned.
steps.tip: You are after color here, not doneness.

steps.text: Pour the green sauce over the chicken — it will hiss and spatter — then add the broth and scrape the bottom of the pot clean.
Simmer uncovered over medium-low, stirring occasionally, until the sauce shifts from grass green to a deeper olive and thickens enough to coat the chicken.
steps.tip: That color change is your cue that the raw edge has cooked out.

steps.text: While it simmers, warm the tortillas one at a time in a dry skillet until they puff, soften and speckle, then stack them inside a folded towel.
Shred the chicken into big rough pieces with two forks right in the pot, stir it back through the sauce, and season with salt to taste.
Heat the rice pouch, then ladle the jocon over it with the warm tortillas alongside for scooping.

swap: No salsa verde on the shelf? Simmer a pound of quartered tomatillos with a jalapeno until soft and blend that in instead.
leftovers: The sauce tightens overnight, so loosen it with a splash of broth; it makes an excellent filling for tacos or enchiladas.

title: Big-Batch Andalusian Sherry-Garlic Chicken with Saffron Potatoes
blurb: Two whole heads of garlic melt into a golden sherry and saffron braise with green olives, cumin and lemon — Seville tavern food, scaled up.

ingredients.item: 4 lb bone-in skin-on Kirkwood chicken thighs
2 heads garlic, cloves peeled and smashed

steps.text: Heat the oven to 400F. Pat the chicken bone-dry and salt it heavily on both sides, then let it sit uncovered while the oven comes up to temperature.
steps.tip: Dry skin is the only route to crisp skin.

steps.text: Crumble the saffron threads into 1/2 cup warm water and leave them to bloom into a deep orange infusion.
Heat 2 tbsp olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and sear the chicken skin-side down in two batches until the skin is bronzed and lifts away without sticking.
steps.tip: Two unhurried batches beat one crowded, steamy one.

steps.text: Move the chicken to a plate. Pour off all but a slick of the fat, add the onion and smashed garlic, and cook over medium until the garlic is soft and golden through, stirring so nothing catches.
steps.tip: Burnt garlic will sour the whole pot.

steps.text: Stir in the cumin and bay leaves for a minute, then pour in the sherry and scrape up every browned bit. Boil hard until the sharp alcohol smell has burned off and the liquid looks syrupy.
Add the potatoes and the saffron water, season with salt, and nestle the chicken back in skin-side up so the skin sits above the liquid.
Slide the uncovered pot into the oven and roast until the potatoes are tender all the way through, the sauce has reduced around them, and the chicken pulls easily from the bone.
steps.tip: Baste the potatoes if you like, but never the skin.

steps.text: Scatter the olives over the top and return the pot to the oven just long enough to heat them through and soften them slightly.
Off the heat, stir the sherry vinegar and lemon juice into the pan sauce, taste for salt, and finish with the lemon zest and parsley.

swap: No sherry — use dry white wine plus an extra tablespoon of sherry vinegar stirred in at the end.
leftovers: Pull the meat off the bones and keep it in the sauce for up to four days; it reheats into a fantastic bocadillo filling.

title: Hunan Farmhouse Pork with Blistered Green Chilies
blurb: Thin-sliced pork seared hard and tossed with wok-blistered chilies, fermented black beans, and a hail of crunchy chili onion.

ingredients.item: 1 lb pork shoulder or thick-cut boneless pork chops
6 long green Anaheim or Hatch chilies, seeded and cut on a sharp bias
2 tbsp salted fermented black beans, rinsed and roughly chopped (or black bean garlic sauce)
1 tbsp Chinese black vinegar or rice vinegar
Neutral oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Put the pork in the freezer for 10 minutes to firm up, then slice it against the grain as thin as you can manage. Toss the slices with 1 tbsp of the soy sauce and a heavy grind of black pepper.
steps.tip: Half-frozen meat is the only way to get paper-thin slices with a home knife.

steps.text: Set a carbon steel or heavy stainless skillet over your highest heat and let it preheat dry for 2 minutes, until the surface looks dull and the first wisp of smoke lifts off. Slice the chilies, garlic, and ginger while it heats.
steps.tip: Open a window before you blister chilies.

steps.text: Add a slick of oil and lay the pork out in a single layer. Sear undisturbed for 3 minutes, until the edges curl and the undersides are brown and lacquered, then toss once and scrape it onto a plate.
steps.tip: Two batches beats one crowded gray one.

steps.text: Add another spoonful of oil and dump in the chilies. Leave them mostly alone over high heat for 4 minutes, until the skins are streaked black and blistered and the flesh has slumped.
Push the chilies to one side, add the garlic, ginger, and fermented black beans to the bare metal, and stir for 1 minute until the garlic goes pale gold and the whole pan smells salty and savory.
steps.tip: Any darker than gold and the garlic turns bitter.

steps.text: Return the pork and its juices, add the remaining soy sauce, the vinegar, and the sugar, and toss hard for 2 minutes until the liquid has nearly vanished and everything wears a glossy coat. Heat the jasmine rice in the microwave while you toss.
Kill the heat and fold in the scallion batons and the Crunchy Chili Onion so the crunch survives. Pile it over the hot rice and spoon the pan drippings on top.
steps.tip: Adding chili onion off-heat keeps the fried garlic bits crisp.

swap: If Hatch or Anaheim chilies are gone, use shishitos or a mix of poblano and jalapeno for the same blistered sweetness and heat.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated; reheat in a ripping-hot dry skillet, or chop it into leftover rice with a beaten egg for fried rice.

title: Chettinad Pepper Chicken with Curry Leaves
blurb: Chicken thighs browned in coconut oil and coated in a coarse fennel-and-black-pepper masala that crackles with fried curry leaves.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb Kirkwood boneless chicken thighs, cut into large bite-size pieces
1 tbsp ginger-garlic paste (or 4 cloves garlic and a thumb of ginger, grated)
2 tsp Kashmiri chili powder or sweet paprika
3 tbsp Friendly Farms plain Greek yogurt
Coconut or olive oil, kosher salt

steps.text: Toss the chicken with the yogurt, turmeric, half the chili powder, and a big pinch of salt until every piece is slicked yellow. Leave it on the counter for 10 minutes while you prep everything else.

Toast the peppercorns, fennel, and coriander in a dry skillet over medium for 2 minutes, shaking constantly, until the fennel darkens a shade and the pepper smells sharp and piney. Crush them coarsely in a mortar or under the bottom of a heavy pan.
steps.tip: Coarse, not powdered — you want to bite into the pepper.

steps.text: Wipe the pan, add 2 tbsp coconut oil, and heat over medium-high. Strip in the curry leaves and stand back for 1 minute while they crackle, curl, and turn glassy.
Add the sliced onion with a pinch of salt and cook for 8 minutes, stirring now and then, until it collapses and the edges go deep brown. Crush the rest of your spices while you wait.
Stir in the ginger-garlic paste and the remaining chili powder and cook 1 minute, until the raw garlic smell burns off and the oil at the edge of the pan turns red.
Spread the marinated chicken into a single layer and leave it completely alone for 5 minutes, until the undersides are browned and release from the pan without tearing.
steps.tip: Resist stirring — that first sear is where the flavor lives.

steps.text: Add the tomato and two-thirds of the crushed pepper masala with a splash of water, cover, and cook 10 minutes until the tomato collapses into the sauce and the chicken is opaque throughout.

Uncover, raise the heat, and cook 4 more minutes until the sauce is nearly dry and clinging to the meat. Off the heat, stir in the last of the pepper masala and warm the naan directly over the burner or in the hot pan.
steps.tip: Finishing with raw-toasted pepper keeps the heat bright instead of muddy.

swap: If fresh curry leaves aren't available, leave them out rather than substituting dried ones; Simply Nature chicken breast cut into chunks works if thighs are sold out.
leftovers: Holds 3 days refrigerated; loosen with a splash of water in a hot skillet, or roll into an L'Oven Fresh Protein Wrap with yogurt and raw onion.

title: Neapolitan Chicken Pizzaiola with Olives and Torn Mozzarella
blurb: Golden cutlets buried in a garlicky oregano tomato sauce studded with capers and olives, then melted over with fresh mozzarella.

ingredients.item: 2 large Simply Nature Organic Chicken Breasts, halved horizontally into 4 thin cutlets
1 can (28 oz) whole peeled San Marzano-style tomatoes
1/2 cup green or black olives, torn open and pitted
Specially Selected olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Pat the cutlets bone dry and season both sides hard with salt and pepper. Film a wide skillet with olive oil and heat over medium-high for 2 minutes, until the oil shimmers and thins out across the pan.
steps.tip: Dry chicken browns; damp chicken steams.

steps.text: Lay the cutlets in without crowding and sear 3 minutes, until the undersides are burnished gold and lift cleanly. Flip, give them 1 more minute, and move them to a plate — they should still be pink inside.
Drop the heat to medium and add the garlic and pepper flakes to the browned fond. Stir for 1 minute, only until the garlic turns blond at the edges and smells sweet.
steps.tip: Browned garlic will make the whole sauce bitter.

steps.text: Crush the tomatoes into the pan through your fingers, add the oregano and a big pinch of salt, and simmer uncovered for 12 minutes. It's ready when it darkens to brick red and orange oil pools around the edge. Tear the mozzarella into rough pieces while it cooks.
steps.tip: Rubbing the dried oregano between your palms as it goes in wakes it up.

steps.text: Stir in the olives and capers, then taste for salt — between the two, it may need none at all.

Nestle the cutlets and any collected juices back into the sauce, drape the torn mozzarella over the top, cover, and cook on low for 5 minutes until the cheese slumps into puddles and the chicken is opaque at its thickest point.
Rest it off the heat for 3 minutes, then tear the basil over the top and drizzle with raw olive oil. Serve straight from the pan with torn ciabatta for the sauce.

swap: Chicken thighs or thin pork cutlets slot straight in; in a pinch use Specially Selected pasta sauce, but simmer it hard for 10 minutes with extra oregano first.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days; pile it cold onto toasted bread, or chop and toss with Priano pasta and a splash of the cooking water.

title: Dominican Pollo Guisado with Green Olives
blurb: Chicken lacquered in burnt-sugar caramel and braised down with sofrito, oregano, and briny olives into a sauce you'll want on everything.

ingredients.item: 4 lb Kirkwood bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks
2 tbsp adobo-style all-purpose seasoning (or 21 Seasoning Salute plus garlic powder)
1 bunch cilantro, stems minced and leaves reserved
1 cup pimiento-stuffed green olives, plus 2 tbsp of their brine
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut into big chunks
3 pouches Earthly Grains long grain rice
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper, water

steps.text: Toss the chicken with the adobo seasoning, oregano, minced cilantro stems, the juice of one lime, salt, and pepper until every piece is coated. Let it sit for 15 minutes while you chop the garlic and potatoes.
steps.tip: Getting seasoning under the skin pays off later.

steps.text: Set a wide Dutch oven over medium heat with 2 tbsp oil and the sugar. Leave it alone for 3 minutes, swirling only once, until the sugar melts and turns the color of an old penny and smells like caramel.
steps.tip: Past dark amber it turns bitter — pull it the second it goes copper.

steps.text: Add the chicken skin-side down in batches without crowding and sear 5 minutes per batch, until the caramel and fat have lacquered the skin a glossy deep brown. Move each batch to a sheet pan.
Dump the fire roasted peppers and onions straight from the bag into the pot and cook 5 minutes over medium-high, until their water boils off and they start to sizzle and catch color.
Stir in the garlic and tomato paste and cook 2 minutes, scraping constantly, until the paste darkens to brick and coats the vegetables.
Return the chicken with any juices, add the olives and their brine, and pour in enough water to come halfway up the meat. Bring it to a boil, then drop to a bare simmer, cover, and cook 25 minutes.

Add the potatoes, uncover, and simmer 20 minutes more, until a knife slides into a potato with no resistance and the sauce has reduced enough to coat the back of a spoon. Heat the rice pouches near the end.
steps.tip: Mash one potato into the sauce to thicken it fast.

steps.text: Pull it off the heat, squeeze in the second lime, and shower with the cilantro leaves. Let it settle for 10 minutes so the sauce tightens, then spoon it over the rice.

swap: Bone-in chicken breast halves or Never Any! drumsticks work fine; a diced onion and two bell peppers replace the frozen peppers and onions.
leftovers: Keeps 4 days refrigerated and freezes well; shred the meat back into the sauce and pile it into Casa Mamita tortillas or over more rice.

title: Laotian Larb Gai with Toasted Rice Powder
blurb: Crumbled chicken drenched in lime and fish sauce, loaded with mint and shallot, and made gritty-crunchy with hand-toasted rice powder.

ingredients.item: 3 tbsp uncooked jasmine or sticky rice
1 to 2 tsp toasted Thai chili flakes
3 shallots or 1/2 red onion, sliced paper thin
1 head butter or romaine lettuce, leaves separated

steps.text: Toast the raw rice in a dry skillet over medium heat for 8 minutes, shaking almost constantly, until every grain is the color of weak tea and the pan smells like popcorn. Tip it onto a plate to cool.
steps.tip: This is the whole dish — don't rush it pale.

steps.text: Grind the cooled rice to the texture of coarse sand in a mortar, spice grinder, or under a heavy pan on a cutting board.

Add a few tablespoons of water and the ground chicken to the same skillet over medium-high and break it into fine crumbles with a spatula. Cook 7 minutes, until no pink remains and the liquid has mostly cooked off.
steps.tip: Poaching in a splash of water keeps the meat tender instead of pebbly.

steps.text: Kill the heat and let the chicken sit for 3 minutes so it stops steaming. Slice the shallots and scallions while you wait.
Whisk the fish sauce, the juice of two limes, the sugar, and the chili flakes until the sugar dissolves. Taste it — it should hit sour first, salty second, hot last.
Pour the dressing over the warm chicken and toss with the shallots and scallions until every crumble is coated and the shallots soften slightly.

Fold in the mint, cilantro, and most of the rice powder right before you serve, then taste and correct with the last lime or more fish sauce. Pile it onto a platter with the lettuce leaves and cucumber spears and dust with the remaining rice powder.
steps.tip: Add the rice powder at the last second or it goes soggy.

swap: Ground pork or turkey works just as well; if there's no fresh mint, double the cilantro rather than reaching for dried.
leftovers: Best within 2 days; wake it up with fresh lime and a handful of new herbs, or wrap it in lettuce with cold rice.

title: Swedish Meatballs in Allspice Cream with Pickled Cucumber
blurb: Tender allspice-and-nutmeg meatballs swimming in a silky pan gravy, cut by sharp vinegar cucumbers and a spoonful of lingonberry.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
1 small yellow onion, grated on a box grater
1 tsp ground allspice plus several scrapes of nutmeg
1/4 cup white vinegar and 1 tbsp sugar
1/3 cup lingonberry or red currant jam
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Shave the cucumber into near-transparent coins and toss with the vinegar, sugar, a big pinch of salt, and the chopped dill stems. Leave it to pickle for 20 minutes, tossing once, until the slices go limp and translucent.
Soak the panko in 1/3 cup of the cream for 5 minutes, until it looks like wet sand and no dry crumbs remain.
steps.tip: This soaked-bread trick is what keeps them soft.

steps.text: Mix the beef, soaked panko, grated onion, allspice and nutmeg, and a generous amount of salt and pepper with your hands just until it comes together. Roll into about twenty walnut-sized balls with damp hands.
steps.tip: Overmixing makes them bouncy instead of tender.

steps.text: Melt 1 tbsp of the butter with a little oil in a wide skillet over medium heat and add the meatballs with space between them. Leave them undisturbed for 5 minutes, until a dark brown crust forms on the underside.
Roll them around the pan and cook 5 minutes more, until browned on all sides and springy to a poke. Move them to a plate.
Melt the remaining butter in the same pan over medium and whisk in the flour. Cook 2 minutes, whisking, until the paste turns pale tan and smells toasty rather than raw.
Pour in the broth in a steady stream while whisking, then the rest of the cream. Simmer 5 minutes until it coats a spoon and a finger drawn across leaves a clean line.
steps.tip: If it tightens too much, loosen it with a splash of broth.

steps.text: Return the meatballs and any juices, cover, and simmer 5 minutes until cooked through and glossy. Shower with torn dill and serve with the drained pickles and a spoonful of jam on each plate.

swap: Half beef and half ground pork is the traditional mix; red currant jelly or even cranberry sauce stands in for lingonberry.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days; reheat gently with a splash of broth so the gravy doesn't split, and serve over mashed potatoes or buttered noodles.

title: Bolivian Silpancho with Fried Eggs and Llajua
blurb: A breadcrumb-crusted steak pounded thin as a tortilla over rice and crisp potatoes, topped with runny eggs and fiery raw chile salsa.

ingredients.item: 1 lb thin-cut sirloin or top round steaks
2 pouches Earthly Grains long grain rice
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Make the llajua first: chop or briefly pulse the tomatoes, chiles, garlic, and half the cilantro into a loose, chunky salsa with the lime juice and plenty of salt. Let it sit and get juicy while you cook.
steps.tip: Leave the chile seeds in — llajua is supposed to bite.

steps.text: Lay each steak between sheets of plastic wrap and pound with the flat of a heavy pan until it's the thickness of a tortilla and nearly translucent at the edges. Season both sides with the cumin, salt, and pepper.
Press each steak firmly into the breadcrumbs on both sides so they stick in one solid layer, then set them on a rack while you cook the potatoes.

Fry the potatoes in a film of oil in a large skillet over medium-high for 10 minutes, turning only two or three times, until they're deeply golden and crisp on the flat sides. Salt them and move them to a plate.
steps.tip: Turning them constantly is what keeps potatoes pale and soft.

steps.text: Add more oil to the same pan and fry the steaks one at a time over medium-high, 2 minutes per side, until the crust is crackly and deep golden. Slice the red onion thin while they cook.
Heat the rice pouches, then fry the eggs in the same skillet over medium for 3 minutes, until the whites are set with lacy brown edges and the yolks still wobble.
Press the hot rice into a small bowl and invert it onto each plate. Lay a steak alongside it and heap the crisp potatoes over the top.
Crown each plate with two fried eggs, scatter the raw onion and remaining cilantro, and spoon llajua over everything. Break the yolks at the table and eat immediately.

swap: If sirloin is out, pound Simply Nature chicken breast cutlets just as thin and bread them the same way.
leftovers: Best fresh, but holds 2 days with the salsa stored separately; chop the steak and potatoes into a hash and top with a fresh fried egg.

title: Caldo Gallego with Chorizo, White Beans, and Greens
blurb: A smoky Galician pot of pork, chorizo, and white beans simmered until the broth turns orange with pimenton and the greens go silky.

ingredients.item: 1 1/2 lb boneless pork shoulder, cut into 1-inch cubes
12 oz Spanish-style chorizo or Never Any! smoked sausage, sliced thick
6 oz Appleton Farms thick-cut bacon, diced
3 cans (15 oz) cannellini or great northern beans, drained and rinsed
1 1/2 lb Yukon gold potatoes, cut into rough chunks
1 lb collard greens, turnip greens, or kale, stemmed and torn
Olive oil, kosher salt, black pepper

steps.text: Render the diced bacon in a large Dutch oven over medium heat for 5 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the fat has pooled and the edges are browning. Lift it out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat behind.
Season the pork hard with salt and pepper and brown it in the bacon fat in two batches, 5 minutes per batch, leaving it undisturbed until a real crust forms. Move it to a bowl.
steps.tip: Crowded pork boils in its own juice and never browns.

steps.text: Add the chorizo and cook 4 minutes, until the edges curl and the fat runs bright orange. Scoop it out and pour off all but about 2 tbsp of the fat.
steps.tip: That orange fat is the color of the whole soup — keep it.

steps.text: Cook the onions over medium for 8 minutes, scraping up the browned bits, until soft and translucent. Stem and tear the greens while they cook.
Pull the pot off the heat, add the garlic and pimenton, and stir for 1 minute so the paprika blooms in the hot fat without scorching.
steps.tip: Paprika burns in seconds over direct heat and turns acrid.

steps.text: Return the pork, bacon, and chorizo, add the broth and bay leaves, and bring to a boil. Drop to a low simmer, cover, and cook 25 minutes until the pork gives easily to a fork.
Add the potatoes and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes, until a knife tip slides through with no resistance and the broth has reduced slightly.

Stir in the beans and the greens a handful at a time, then simmer 10 minutes until the greens are fully tender and the broth is cloudy and rich. Mash a few potatoes against the side of the pot, fish out the bay leaves, and season with salt.
steps.tip: Mashing a little potato thickens it without any flour.

swap: Smoked ham hock or diced ham can replace the bacon, and any sturdy green — kale, chard, even cabbage — stands in for turnip greens.
leftovers: Keeps 5 days refrigerated and freezes for months; it thickens overnight, so loosen with broth and expect it to taste better on day two.

title: Beijing Zhajiangmian: Fried Bean Sauce Pork Noodles
blurb: A dark, glossy heap of slow-fried pork and fermented bean paste dropped onto springy wheat noodles with a cold thicket of raw cucumber, tossed at the table until every strand turns mahogany.

ingredients.item: 1 tbsp Trader Joe's Crunchy Chili Onion
6 scallions, whites and greens sliced and kept separate
4 garlic cloves, minced, plus a 1-inch knob of ginger, grated
1 tbsp Shaoxing wine or dry sherry
10 oz fresh or dried wheat noodles (Fusia)
1 English cucumber, cut into long matchsticks

steps.text: Whisk the hoisin, miso, soy sauce, Shaoxing wine, sugar, and 1/3 cup water in a bowl until completely smooth, then park it next to the stove. Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil for the noodles.
steps.tip: Pre-mixing keeps the paste from scorching when it hits the pan.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a wok or heavy skillet over medium-high until it shimmers, add the pork, and press it into one flat slab. Leave it completely alone until the underside is deep golden and crusted, then break it into rough crumbles.
steps.tip: Resist stirring, the crust is where the flavor comes from.

steps.text: Push the pork to one side, drop the scallion whites, garlic, and ginger into the rendered fat, and stir until fragrant and just softened. Fold everything together.

Pour in the sauce, lower the heat to medium-low, and let it bubble lazily, stirring every couple of minutes, until it darkens to glossy mahogany and a slick of red oil separates around the edge. Cut the cucumber into matchsticks while it cooks.
steps.tip: Long and slow is what makes it taste roasted instead of raw.

steps.text: Boil the noodles until just chewy at the center, then scoop out 1/2 cup of the cooking water before draining. Rinse the noodles briefly under cold water so they stay bouncy.

Stir the sesame oil and Crunchy Chili Onion into the sauce, then loosen it with splashes of noodle water until it slides off the spoon in a thick ribbon. Taste and add a pinch of salt only if it needs it, the miso is already salty.

Divide the noodles between two deep bowls, spoon a generous mound of sauce into the center of each, and pile the cucumber and scallion greens around the rim. Bring them to the table unmixed and toss hard right before eating.
steps.tip: Mixing at the table is the tradition, not a shortcut.

swap: No miso? Use an extra 3 tbsp hoisin plus 1 tsp Fusia soy sauce and skip the sugar entirely.
leftovers: The sauce keeps 5 days refrigerated and thickens into a paste, so loosen it with hot water in the pan and boil fresh noodles.

title: Gujarati Kadhi with Crisped Paneer
blurb: A silky sweet-sour yogurt curry that hits sugar first, tang second, and a slow chile hum last, finished with a spitting ghee tempering poured over crisp-edged cubes of paneer.

ingredients.item: 1 1/2 cups Friendly Farms plain whole-milk yogurt
1 tbsp jaggery or dark brown sugar
2 dried red chiles and 1 tsp grated ginger
1 pouch Earthly Grains basmati rice and 1/2 cup chopped cilantro

steps.text: Whisk the yogurt, chickpea flour, turmeric, jaggery, 1 tsp salt, and 2 cups water in a bowl until it is absolutely lump-free and thin as heavy cream. Run your finger along the bottom of the bowl to check for hidden pockets of flour.
steps.tip: Any lump of besan will taste raw and chalky later.

steps.text: Pat the paneer dry and sear it in 1 tbsp of the ghee in a nonstick skillet over medium-high, turning once, until two sides are deep golden and the edges look crisp. Slide it onto a plate and salt it lightly.
steps.tip: Wet paneer will stick and tear instead of browning.

steps.text: Pour the yogurt mixture into a saucepan and bring it to a bare simmer over medium, whisking constantly in one direction until it thickens slightly and loses its raw, chalky smell.
steps.tip: Constant motion is what keeps the yogurt from splitting.

steps.text: Drop the heat to low and let it simmer uncovered, stirring every couple of minutes, until it coats the back of a spoon and tastes silky rather than floury. It should look like thin cream, not gravy.
Make the vaghar: melt the remaining ghee in a small skillet over medium-high, add the mustard seeds, and hold a lid partly over the pan until they pop like rain against it.
steps.tip: Wait for the popping to slow, that is your cue.

steps.text: Add the cumin seeds, dried chiles, curry leaves, ginger, and asafoetida and stand back, the leaves will crackle violently. Swirl for about twenty seconds until everything smells nutty, then pour the whole spitting mixture straight into the kadhi.
steps.tip: Pour it in while it is still sizzling audibly.

steps.text: Taste for the Gujarati balance, sweet arriving first and sour right behind it, adjusting with a pinch more jaggery or salt. Heat the rice pouch, ladle the kadhi over it, add the paneer, and shower with cilantro.

swap: No curry leaves? Skip them and add an extra 1/2 tsp cumin seeds plus a wide strip of lime zest to the tempering.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days refrigerated and sets thick when cold, so reheat gently over low heat with a splash of water and never let it boil.

title: Saltimbocca alla Romana with Skillet Artichokes
blurb: Pounded cutlets pinned with sage and prosciutto that crisps into salty lace, deglazed with white wine and butter, alongside artichokes browned hard in the second pan.

ingredients.item: 2 large Simply Nature organic chicken breasts, halved horizontally into 4 cutlets
1 jar Trader Joe's Quartered Marinated Artichokes, drained well

steps.text: Pound the cutlets between two sheets of plastic to an even 1/4 inch and season them with black pepper only, since the prosciutto brings plenty of salt. Lay two sage leaves on each, drape a slice of prosciutto over the top, and press it down firmly with your palm.
steps.tip: Even thickness means every cutlet finishes at the same moment.

steps.text: Dust only the bare chicken side in flour and shake off every bit of excess, leaving the prosciutto naked. Drain the artichokes and blot them dry on a towel while you work.
steps.tip: Flour on the ham would stop it from crisping.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil with 1 tbsp of the butter in a large skillet over medium-high until the foam subsides, then lay the cutlets in prosciutto side down. Cook without moving them until the ham is bronzed, crisp, and welded to the meat.
steps.tip: Press each cutlet gently for full contact.

steps.text: Flip and cook until the chicken is opaque and springs back when pressed, then move them to warm plates. Meanwhile set a second skillet over medium-high with 1 tbsp oil and the smashed garlic.
Lay the artichokes cut side down in the second pan and leave them completely still until the flat faces are browned and blistered, then toss once and kill the heat.
steps.tip: They will spit, so keep a lid handy.

steps.text: Pour the wine into the empty chicken pan over medium-high and scrape up every brown fleck as it bubbles, reducing until it turns syrupy and just coats the back of a spoon.

Pull the pan off the heat, swirl in the remaining butter and a squeeze of lemon until the sauce turns glossy, and spoon it over the cutlets. Toss the artichokes with the parsley, parmesan, and another squeeze of lemon and pile them alongside.
steps.tip: Off-heat butter is what makes the sauce shine instead of break.

swap: No marinated artichokes? Blister a bag of Season's Choice green beans in the same pan with the garlic instead.
leftovers: Best straight from the pan, but leftover cutlets are excellent cold the next day, sliced over greens with lemon and olive oil.

title: Seco de Pollo: Ecuadorian Beer-Braised Chicken
blurb: Chicken braised until it slides off the bone in a blended cilantro-and-beer sauce that cooks down from shocking green to deep olive, brightened with lime-pickled red onion.

ingredients.item: 4 lb bone-in skin-on chicken thighs and drumsticks (Kirkwood)
2 large bunches cilantro, stems and all
2 tsp achiote (annatto) powder or smoked paprika
1 tbsp dark brown sugar or grated panela
3 pouches Earthly Grains long grain rice
1 red onion, thinly sliced, and 3 limes

steps.text: Blend the cilantro, garlic, beer, cumin, achiote, and 1 tsp salt until you have a smooth, violently green liquid. Pat the chicken bone dry and season it all over with salt and pepper.
steps.tip: Use the cilantro stems, they carry most of the flavor.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high until it shimmers, then brown the chicken skin side down in two batches without crowding, until the skin is deep gold and releases from the pot on its own. Move it to a plate.
steps.tip: If it sticks, it is not ready to turn.

steps.text: Pour off all but 2 tbsp of the fat, drop the heat to medium, and cook the yellow onions and bell pepper with a pinch of salt, scraping up the fond, until they are limp and edged with gold.
steps.tip: This refrito is the backbone of the whole pot.

steps.text: Add the tomatoes and brown sugar and cook, stirring often, until the tomatoes collapse and the mixture darkens and turns jammy enough to leave a trail behind the spoon.
Pour in the green blend and bring it to a simmer, then nestle the chicken back in skin side up along with any juices from the plate. It will look alarmingly bright, but it dulls to olive as it cooks.

Cover partially and simmer over low, adjusting the flame so the surface only blips, until the meat pulls away from the bone with a fork. While it braises, toss the sliced red onion with the juice of 2 limes and a big pinch of salt so it softens and turns pink.
steps.tip: A hard boil will toughen the chicken and dull the herbs.

steps.text: Uncover, raise the heat to medium, and reduce until the sauce is glossy and thick enough to cling to the pieces rather than pool around them. Taste and correct with salt and a squeeze of lime.
Heat the rice pouches and serve the chicken over rice with plenty of sauce spooned across, topped with the pickled onions and the remaining lime cut into wedges.
steps.tip: The acid on top is what keeps the rich sauce moving.

swap: No lager? Use 1 1/2 cups chicken broth plus 1 tbsp Fusia rice vinegar for a similar bright tang.
leftovers: Refrigerates 4 days and freezes 3 months; the sauce tightens when cold, so reheat covered with a splash of water.

title: Beef Lok Lak with Tuk Meric
blurb: Cubes of steak seared black in spots and glazed sticky, piled on a cold tomato salad under a runny fried egg, with a fiercely sour lime-and-black-pepper dip for every bite.

ingredients.item: 1 1/4 lb sirloin or flat iron steak, cut into 1-inch cubes
1 head green leaf lettuce, 1 tomato sliced, and 1/2 red onion sliced paper-thin

steps.text: Toss the beef with the oyster sauce, soy sauce, fish sauce, sugar, half the garlic, and 1 tbsp of the cracked pepper until every cube is slick. Let it sit at room temperature while you build the rest.
steps.tip: Cracked, not ground, so you get gritty pops of pepper.

steps.text: Make the tuk meric by stirring the juice of 2 limes with the remaining cracked pepper, remaining garlic, and 1 tsp salt in a small bowl. Taste it, it should be aggressively sour, salty, and hot enough to make you blink.
steps.tip: This dip is the dish, do not tone it down.

steps.text: Line two plates with the lettuce, sliced tomato, and red onion and squeeze half a lime over the top. Heat the rice pouch and keep it covered.

Heat 1 tbsp of the oil in a cast iron skillet over high until it is faintly smoking, then add half the beef in a single layer. Leave it untouched until a dark crust forms on the underside, toss for thirty seconds, and move it to a plate.
steps.tip: Two batches, or the beef steams and goes gray.

steps.text: Repeat with the second half of the beef, then return the first batch and all its juices and toss over high heat until the marinade reduces to a sticky glaze clinging to every cube.
Wipe the skillet, add the remaining oil over medium-high, and fry the eggs until the whites are set with brown lacy edges but the yolks still wobble.
steps.tip: The running yolk becomes part of the sauce.

steps.text: Pile the beef over the salad, slide an egg onto each plate, and serve with rice and the tuk meric alongside for dipping bite by bite.

swap: No steak? Cube 1 1/4 lb Aldi pork loin and sear it exactly the same way, just a minute longer per batch.
leftovers: The beef keeps 3 days; reheat it fast in a screaming skillet and build the salad and dip fresh, since the lime dulls overnight.

title: Kure na Paprice: Czech Paprika Cream Chicken
blurb: Thighs braised in a brick-red sauce built on a shameless amount of sweet paprika, caraway, and marjoram, then finished with cream and tempered sour cream over buttered noodles.

ingredients.item: 1 tsp hot paprika or 1/2 tsp cayenne
1 tsp caraway seeds and 1 tsp dried marjoram

steps.text: Season the thighs hard with salt and pepper. Melt 2 tbsp of the butter in a Dutch oven over medium-high until it foams, then brown the chicken in a single layer on one side only until deeply golden, and move it to a plate.
steps.tip: One good side of color is all you need before braising.

steps.text: Lower the heat to medium, add the onion, the remaining butter, and the caraway seeds, and cook, scraping up the browned bits, until the onion is completely soft and translucent with no crunch left. Put a pot of salted water on to boil while you wait.
Pull the pot entirely off the burner and stir in both paprikas and the marjoram, which should smell sweet and toasty within seconds of hitting the hot fat.
steps.tip: Paprika scorches into bitterness in a hot pan, so work off the heat.

steps.text: Return the pot to medium-low, sprinkle in the flour, and stir until it coats the onions and looks pasty. Whisk in the broth in a steady stream until the sauce is smooth and glossy with no lumps.

Nestle the chicken and its juices back in, cover, and simmer over low until the thighs are fork-tender and the sauce is brick red. Boil the noodles until just tender, drain, and toss them with a pat of butter.
steps.tip: Keep it at a lazy bubble, not a rolling boil.

steps.text: Uncover, pour in the heavy cream, and simmer until the sauce thickens enough that a finger drawn across the back of a spoon leaves a clean line.
Whisk a ladle of the hot sauce into the sour cream in a small bowl until loose, then stir that back into the pot off the heat. Finish with a squeeze of lemon and salt to taste.
steps.tip: Tempering is what keeps the sour cream from curdling into grit.

steps.text: Pile the buttered noodles into shallow bowls, lay the chicken on top, ladle the sauce generously over everything, and grind more black pepper across.

swap: No heavy cream? Use 1 cup Friendly Farms whole milk and add an extra tablespoon of flour at the roux step.
leftovers: Keeps 3 days; reheat over low heat without boiling so the sour cream stays smooth, and cook the noodles fresh.

title: Tico Casado: Pork Chops with Gallo Pinto
blurb: Thick chops lacquered in a tangy, cumin-heavy Lizano-style sauce, plated the Costa Rican way with purple-stained gallo pinto and sticky caramelized plantains.

ingredients.item: 2 thick bone-in pork chops, about 1 1/2 lb total
2 tsp achiote (annatto) powder or smoked paprika
1 (15 oz) can black beans, liquid and all
1 pouch Earthly Grains long grain rice
2 very ripe black-skinned plantains and 1 lime

steps.text: Whisk the Worcestershire, cumin, achiote, brown sugar, half the garlic, and 1/2 tsp black pepper into a thin brown Lizano-style sauce. Rub a third of it over the chops and leave them on the counter while you start the beans.
steps.tip: Room-temperature chops sear far more evenly.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in a skillet over medium and cook the onion, bell pepper, and remaining garlic with a pinch of salt until soft, sweet, and browning at the edges.

Add the black beans with all of their canning liquid plus 2 tbsp of the reserved sauce and simmer until the liquid reduces to a dark, syrupy glaze coating the beans. Heat the rice pouch while it bubbles.
steps.tip: That bean liquid is what dyes the rice, do not drain it.

steps.text: Fold the hot rice into the beans until every grain is stained purple-brown, then stir in half the cilantro and pull the pan off the heat. Cover to keep it warm.
steps.tip: Stained and glossy, never soupy, is the mark of good gallo pinto.

steps.text: Slice the plantains on a sharp diagonal about 1/2 inch thick. Heat 2 tbsp oil in a second skillet over medium and fry them until deep caramel and sticky on both cut faces, then drain on a towel and salt immediately.
steps.tip: Black skins only, yellow plantains will taste starchy.

steps.text: Wipe out the first skillet, raise it to medium-high with 1 tsp oil, and sear the chops undisturbed until a dark crust forms and they lift cleanly from the pan.
Flip, brush with the remaining sauce, and cook until the glaze goes tacky and the meat reaches 140F next to the bone.
steps.tip: Pull them early, they climb several degrees while resting.

steps.text: Rest the chops while you plate the gallo pinto, plantains, and a lime wedge on each plate. Slice the chops thick, lay them alongside, and scrape the pan glaze over the top with the rest of the cilantro.

swap: No ripe plantains? Fry thick rounds of sweet potato in the same oil until the edges caramelize.
leftovers: Gallo pinto is better on day two; reheat it in a skillet with a splash of water and crown it with a fried egg.

title: Me'orav Yerushalmi: Jerusalem Mixed Grill
blurb: Griddle-charred chicken and livers tumbled with frizzled onions and a fistful of cumin, turmeric, and baharat, stuffed into pita with runny tahini and a green streak of zhoug.

ingredients.item: 2 1/2 lb boneless skinless chicken thighs (Kirkwood), sliced into strips
1 lb chicken livers, trimmed and cut into bite-size pieces
2 large onions, halved and thinly sliced
1 tbsp baharat or Trader Joe's 21 Seasoning Salute
6 pita breads and 1 cup sliced dill pickles

steps.text: Slice the thighs into 1/2-inch strips, cut the livers into bite-size pieces, and pat everything very dry. Toss it all with the cumin, turmeric, baharat, coriander, 2 tsp salt, and 1 tsp black pepper until uniformly gold.
steps.tip: Dry meat plus a hot pan gives char instead of steam.

steps.text: Heat 1 tbsp oil in your largest skillet over medium-high until it just begins to smoke, spread half the chicken in a single layer, and leave it alone until the underside is browned and the spices smell toasted. Toss for a minute, then transfer to a bowl.
steps.tip: Crowding the pan is the one mistake that ruins this.

steps.text: Sear the second batch of chicken the same way while you slice the onions, then add it to the bowl.

Add another tablespoon of oil and all the onions with a pinch of salt to the empty skillet over medium-high, scraping up the spiced fond as they release moisture. Cook until they collapse and take on frizzled brown edges.
steps.tip: Those stuck-on spices are the whole point of the pan.

steps.text: Push the onions to the side, drop in the butter, and sear the livers hard until browned outside and barely pink at the center.
steps.tip: Overcooked livers turn chalky, so pull them early.

steps.text: Return all the chicken and its collected juices, add the juice of one lemon and 1/4 cup water, and toss over high heat until the liquid cooks away and everything is glossy and coated.
Whisk the tahini with the juice of the second lemon, a pinch of salt, and cold water added a splash at a time. It will seize into a stiff pale paste first, then loosen into a pourable ivory sauce.
steps.tip: It always seizes, keep adding water and keep whisking.

steps.text: Warm the pitas directly over a burner or in a dry pan until they puff and blister, then stuff them with the grill, drizzle heavily with tahini and zhoug, and tuck pickles down the side.

swap: Squeamish about livers? Use another pound of chicken thighs and add an extra teaspoon of baharat for depth.
leftovers: The meat keeps 4 days and freezes 2 months; reheat it in a dry, ripping-hot skillet to bring the crisp edges back rather than microwaving.

title: Macanese Minchi with Crispy Potatoes and Fried Eggs
blurb: Macau's great comfort dish: soy-and-Worcestershire beef tangled with craggy fried potato cubes and crowned with a lacy fried egg.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Simply Nature Organic Grass-Fed Ground Beef
3 cups Season's Choice frozen diced breakfast potatoes
3 tbsp Fusia Asian Inspirations soy sauce
1 tsp Mushroom & Company Multipurpose Umami Seasoning Blend

steps.text: Film a large nonstick skillet with olive oil and set it over medium-high until the surface shimmers and thins out. Scatter the frozen potatoes in a single loose layer and walk away so the undersides can blister and turn deep gold.
steps.tip: Crowding steams them

steps.text: Toss the potatoes and keep cooking until most faces are crackly and browned, then scrape them onto a plate and salt them while they are hot. Dice the onion and mince the garlic while they finish.
Return the empty skillet to medium-high, add the beef, and press it into one flat slab. Leave it completely undisturbed until the underside forms a dark brown crust that releases from the pan.

Break the beef into rough pebbles with a wooden spoon, then add the onion, garlic, and bay leaves. Stir often until the onion turns translucent at the edges and the garlic smells toasty rather than sharp.

Pour in the soy sauce and Worcestershire, then sprinkle over the brown sugar and umami seasoning. Simmer over medium until the liquid tightens into a dark glaze that clings to the meat instead of pooling.
steps.tip: Glaze, don't drown

steps.text: While the beef glazes, microwave the frozen jasmine rice according to the bag and fluff it with a fork. Fold the crisped potatoes back into the beef right at the end so they stay crunchy.
In a small nonstick pan over medium heat, fry the eggs in a slick of olive oil until the whites are opaque all the way through and the edges go frilly and brown but the yolks still tremble.
Fish out the bay leaves, spoon the minchi over the rice, and slide an egg onto each plate. Finish with the sliced scallions and a last few drops of Worcestershire.

swap: If the frozen diced potatoes are sold out, cut two russets into small cubes, parboil them for a few minutes, and pat them very dry before frying.
leftovers: Refrigerate the beef and potatoes together up to three days and reheat in a dry hot skillet so the potato edges crisp back up before you fry a fresh egg.

title: Sindhi Seyal Murgh, Smothered in Garlic and Cilantro
blurb: Chicken braised down into a fistful of garlic, split green chilies, and an almost indecent amount of cilantro until the masala clings tight to every piece.

ingredients.item: 1.5 lb Kirkwood boneless skinless chicken thighs, halved
1 large bunch cilantro, tender stems and leaves, roughly chopped
8 cloves garlic, half minced and half smashed
1/2 cup Friendly Farms plain Greek yogurt

steps.text: Pat the chicken very dry, salt it well, and rub it with the turmeric and red chili powder until every piece is stained yellow. Let it sit while you chop the cilantro, garlic, and tomatoes.
steps.tip: Dry chicken, better sear

steps.text: Heat three tablespoons of olive oil in a heavy skillet over medium-high, then add the cumin seeds. Wait until they sizzle steadily, darken a shade, and smell nutty before moving on.
steps.tip: Smell them, don't scorch them

steps.text: Lay the chicken in one uncrowded layer and leave it alone until the undersides are burnished gold and lift cleanly. Flip once and sear the second side.
Add the minced and smashed garlic, the ginger, and the split green chilies. Stir constantly so the garlic goes pale gold and loses its raw bite without burning.
Tip in the tomatoes and crush them against the pan. Cook over medium until they collapse into a thick paste and you see oil beading at the edges of the masala.
steps.tip: Oil separating means the masala is ready

steps.text: Drop the heat to medium-low and stir in the yogurt one spoonful at a time so it never breaks. Cover and simmer until the chicken is fork tender and the sauce has darkened.

Pile in the whole chopped bunch of cilantro and the garam masala, then fold until the greens wilt down and the sauce is thick enough to cling rather than run. Char the naan in a dry skillet while it finishes.
Let the pan rest off the heat so the masala tightens, then serve straight from the skillet with the hot naan for scooping.

swap: No fresh green chilies at the store? Use a spoonful of Green Dragon Hot Sauce stirred in with the yogurt for the same grassy heat.
leftovers: This tastes even better on day two once the garlic mellows; store it up to three days and reheat gently with a splash of water to loosen the masala.

title: Venetian Shrimp in Saor over Soft Parmesan Polenta
blurb: Sweet-sour saor onions slumped in vinegar with raisins and pine nuts, spooned over seared red shrimp and a warm pool of parmesan polenta.

ingredients.item: 1 lb Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, thawed and peeled
2 large red onions, halved and sliced thin

steps.text: Warm a generous slick of olive oil in a wide skillet over medium-low, then add the sliced onions, bay leaves, and a big pinch of salt. Cook, stirring now and then, until the onions collapse into soft ribbons that are sweet and barely blond.
steps.tip: Low and slow keeps them sweet, not brown

steps.text: While the onions soften, bring a pot of salted water to a rolling boil for the polenta and pat the shrimp completely dry on paper towels.

Pour the vinegar into the onions and add the raisins and sugar. Simmer until the sharp vinegar smell mellows into something rounded and the pan looks glossy and nearly syrupy, then stir in the pine nuts.
Rain the polenta into the boiling water while whisking hard so no lumps form, then drop the heat to low. Whisk often until it thickens enough to pull away from the side of the pot.
Beat the parmesan and butter into the polenta until it is loose and creamy, taste for salt, and cover it off the heat so it stays soft.

Toss the dry shrimp with the flour, salt, and pepper. Sear them in one layer in a hot oiled skillet over medium-high until they turn coral pink, curl into loose C shapes, and are opaque at the thickest part.
steps.tip: Argentinian reds cook fast, watch closely

steps.text: Kill the heat, spoon the warm saor over the shrimp, and toss so every piece is coated. Let the pan sit so the vinegar and sweetness soak in.
steps.tip: The rest is what makes it saor

steps.text: Spread the polenta across two warm shallow bowls, pile on the shrimp and onions with all their syrup, and scatter the parsley over the top.

swap: If pine nuts are out of stock, slivered almonds toasted in a dry pan give the same sweet crunch against the vinegar.
leftovers: The saor shrimp are traditionally eaten cold the next day; keep them chilled up to two days and eat them straight from the fridge on toasted bread.

title: Honduran Tapado: Garifuna Coconut Chicken and Shrimp Stew
blurb: A Caribbean-coast pot from Honduras where coconut milk simmers gold with cumin and lime until chicken, plantain, and sweet red shrimp fall together.

ingredients.item: 2.5 lb Kirkwood boneless skinless chicken thighs
1 lb Raw Argentinian Red Shrimp, peeled
2 green plantains, peeled and cut into thick coins

steps.text: Season the chicken all over with salt and half the cumin. Heat olive oil in a large Dutch oven over medium-high and brown the thighs in two batches, undisturbed, until each side wears a deep golden crust.
steps.tip: Two batches, or it steams

steps.text: While the chicken browns, peel and cut the plantains into thick coins and halve the potatoes so everything is ready to go into the pot at once.

Move the browned chicken to a plate, drop the heat to medium, and add the onion, garlic, and fire roasted peppers and onions. Cook, scraping up the brown film on the bottom, until the onion is soft and translucent.
steps.tip: Those scraped-up bits are the flavor

steps.text: Stir in the rest of the cumin, then return the chicken with its juices and add the broth, coconut milk, potatoes, and plantains. Bring it up to a lazy simmer with slow bubbles rather than a hard boil.
steps.tip: A hard boil splits coconut milk

steps.text: Simmer partly covered until a knife slides into the potatoes with no resistance, the plantains turn tender and starchy, and the broth thickens to pale gold. Chop the cilantro and juice the limes while you wait.
Taste for salt, then slip the shrimp under the surface of the stew and cook just until they curl and turn opaque coral through the middle.
steps.tip: Pull them early, the pot keeps cooking

steps.text: Kill the heat and stir in the lime juice and half the cilantro. Let the pot rest so the coconut settles into the broth and the flavors knit together.
Ladle into deep bowls, making sure every serving gets chicken, shrimp, plantain, and potato. Finish with the remaining cilantro and a wedge of lime.

swap: No green plantains in produce? Use a large sweet potato cut into thick chunks and add it with the baby potatoes.
leftovers: Store up to four days; reheat over low heat only until steaming so the shrimp stay tender, and freeze portions before adding the shrimp if you want them perfect later.

title: Balinese Sate Lilit Chicken with Sambal Matah
blurb: Lemongrass and coconut chicken patties charred hard in a skillet, then buried under raw sambal matah that hisses when the hot coconut oil hits it.

steps.text: Mix the ground chicken with the shredded coconut, two tablespoons of the lemongrass paste, the garlic, turmeric, coconut milk, and a heavy pinch of salt. Work it with your hands until it turns tacky and holds its shape when you squeeze a lump, then chill it.
steps.tip: Tacky mix means the patties won't crumble

steps.text: Build the sambal matah while the mixture chills: toss the shallots, chilies, remaining lemongrass paste, the zest and juice of two limes, and salt with your fingertips, bruising the shallots as you go.
steps.tip: Bruise, don't mash

steps.text: Heat the coconut oil in a small pan over medium-high until it ripples and just begins to shimmer, then pour it straight over the sambal so it sizzles on contact and stir it through.
steps.tip: Hot oil wakes the raw shallots up

steps.text: With wet hands, form the chilled chicken into eight oblong patties, pressing them into flat ovals so they sear evenly rather than steam.
Heat a cast iron skillet over medium-high, film it with oil, and lay the patties in without crowding. Leave them completely alone until the undersides build a dark brown, almost charred crust.
Flip, lower the heat to medium, and cook until the patties feel springy in the middle and the juices run clear with no pink at the center.
Heat the frozen jasmine rice while the patties finish, then fluff it and dust it with the Chili Lime Seasoning.
Pile the rice into bowls, lean the charred patties against it, and heap the sambal matah over everything with its oil. Serve with the last lime cut into wedges.

swap: If lemongrass paste is missing, finely mince the pale bottom of two fresh lemongrass stalks, or use the zest of an extra lime plus a little grated ginger.
leftovers: Keep the patties and sambal in separate containers up to three days; reheat the patties in a skillet and spoon the cold sambal over at the last second.

title: Austrian Pork Schnitzel with Warm Vinegar Potato Salad
blurb: Shatteringly crisp, puffed golden schnitzel with a hard squeeze of lemon, next to warm Erdapfelsalat slick with mustard, vinegar, and shaved red onion.

ingredients.item: 1/2 small red onion, shaved paper thin

steps.text: Start the potatoes first: cover them with heavily salted water, bring to a boil, and cook until a knife slides into the middle with no resistance.
steps.tip: Salt the water like soup

steps.text: While they boil, lay the pork between two sheets of plastic wrap and pound it with a heavy pan until each cutlet is thin, even, and noticeably wider than it started.
steps.tip: Even thickness means even frying

steps.text: Set up three shallow dishes with the flour, beaten eggs, and breadcrumbs. Season the pork, then coat each piece in flour, egg, and crumbs, pressing only lightly so the crust can puff away from the meat.
steps.tip: Press hard and the coating glues down

steps.text: Drain the potatoes, slice them into warm coins, and whisk the mustard, vinegar, warm broth, red onion, salt, and pepper together. Pour it over while the potatoes are still steaming and toss, then leave them to soak.
steps.tip: Dress them hot so they drink it up

steps.text: Melt half the butter with a slick of olive oil in a large skillet over medium-high until the foam subsides. Lay in two cutlets and swirl the pan constantly so hot fat washes over the tops and the crust blisters and puffs golden.
steps.tip: Keep the pan moving

steps.text: Flip and fry the second side until it is the deep color of a good pretzel and the edges are crisp and ruffled.
Drain the schnitzel on a wire rack, never on paper, and salt it the second it comes out of the pan. Wipe the skillet, add the remaining butter and oil, and fry the second pair the same way.
steps.tip: A rack keeps the bottom crisp

steps.text: Fold the chives through the potato salad, taste it for vinegar and salt, and serve the schnitzel straight away with lemon wedges to squeeze over the crust.

swap: Thin-cut chicken breasts pounded the same way stand in perfectly, and a spoonful of any berry jam on the side plays the part of lingonberry.
leftovers: The potato salad keeps three days and only gets better; re-crisp leftover schnitzel in a hot dry skillet or oven rather than the microwave.

title: Tunisian Ojja with Merguez and Eggs
blurb: Tunis in a skillet: harissa and crushed caraway fried into tomatoes and peppers with spicy merguez, with eggs poached right in the fiery sauce.

ingredients.item: 12 oz merguez sausage, cut into thick coins

steps.text: Set a wide skillet over medium-high and brown the merguez coins in a bare film of olive oil until they are crusted on both cut sides and the fat runs out bright red.
steps.tip: That red fat is the whole base

steps.text: Lift the sausage out with a slotted spoon and leave the fat behind. Drop the heat to medium, add the garlic, crushed caraway, and coriander, and stir until they smell toasted but the garlic has not colored.
Stir in the tomato paste and harissa and fry them in the fat, pressing them against the pan, until the paste darkens to brick red and smells roasted instead of raw.
steps.tip: Frying the paste kills the tinny taste

steps.text: Add the fire roasted peppers and onions and the diced tomatoes with their juice. Simmer over medium until the sauce thickens enough that a spoon dragged through it leaves a trail that holds. Slice the bread and chop the parsley while it reduces.
Return the sausage and any resting juices, taste for salt, and make four shallow wells in the sauce with the back of a spoon. Crack an egg into each well and season the yolks.
Cover the pan and cook over medium-low until the whites are fully opaque and set but the yolks still wobble when you nudge the handle.
steps.tip: Pull it early, carryover finishes the yolks

steps.text: Shower the whole skillet with parsley and squeeze lemon over the top. Bring it to the table in the pan with the bread for dragging through the sauce.

swap: No merguez on the counter? Use Never Any! spicy sausage and add an extra spoonful of harissa plus a pinch more caraway to get the same North African punch.
leftovers: The sauce alone keeps four days and freezes well; reheat it in a skillet and poach fresh eggs in it rather than saving the cooked ones.

title: Bahamian Brown Stew Chicken with Thyme and Hot Pepper
blurb: Nassau-style stew chicken, where sugar burnt almost to bitterness lacquers the meat mahogany before it simmers soft with thyme, allspice, and hot sauce.

ingredients.item: 3.5 lb Kirkwood bone-in chicken thighs and drumsticks

steps.text: Season the chicken hard on all sides with salt, pepper, the thyme, and the allspice, then let it sit out while you slice the onion, pepper, and celery.
steps.tip: Season early, season heavily

steps.text: In a wide Dutch oven over medium-high, stir the brown sugar into a thin film of olive oil and swirl until it melts, foams up, and turns the color of dark coffee with a faintly bitter smell.
steps.tip: This burnt sugar is the color of the whole dish

steps.text: Immediately lay in the chicken skin side down in batches, standing back because it will spit, and brown it hard, turning once, until each piece is lacquered mahogany.
Move the chicken to a tray and add the onion, bell pepper, celery, and bay leaves to the pot. Cook, scraping the dark caramel off the bottom, until the vegetables soften and go glossy.
Stir in the tomato paste and hot sauce and cook until the paste turns brick colored and coats the vegetables.

Return the chicken with every drop of its juice, add the potatoes, and pour in enough water to come halfway up the chicken. Bring it to a simmer, cover, and cook until the meat pulls easily from the bone. Heat the rice pouches near the end.
Uncover, raise the heat to medium-high, and let the liquid boil down until the gravy is dark and thick enough to coat the back of a spoon.
steps.tip: Taste for salt only after it reduces

steps.text: Rest the pot off the heat, fish out the bay leaves, and skim any fat from the surface. Spoon the chicken and gravy over the hot rice.

swap: If bone-in pieces are picked over, boneless thighs work; brown them the same way and cut the covered simmer roughly in half.
leftovers: This deepens overnight and keeps four days; pull the meat off the bones and reheat it in the gravy, or freeze it in portions for up to three months.
